📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Built with leading asset managers and already live with their investors, Anduin Investor Portal delivers a fully white-labeled experience that connects fundraising, onboarding, reporting, and ongoing communications, supported by AI-powered workflows.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Anduin today opened its Investor Portal to all. Developed with leading asset managers and already live with their investors, the fully white-labeled portal connects fundraising, onboarding, reporting, and ongoing servicing in one experience, supported by AI-powered workflows.

Built on Anduin's intelligent operating platform and fully integrated with Fund Subscription and Investor Data Management, the portal carries investor records, contacts, and permissions from onboarding into ongoing servicing. AI-powered workflows help teams and fund administrators distribute documents across entities and contacts, while recording communications and profile updates for an audit trail.

Engagement analytics show how investors interact with documents, videos, and pages, helping investor relations teams tailor communications and inform conversations ahead of future fundraises.

"An investor portal should do more than check a box. We believe that every interaction the GP has with its investors is an opportunity to deepen that relationship," said Eliot Hodges, CEO of Anduin. "By putting AI to work across connected data and workflows, we're helping firms reduce manual work, deliver best-in-class investor experiences, and scale their operations without adding complexity.".

Anduin's migration experts use a programmatic approach to transfer investor data and documents from legacy portals accurately and efficiently, reducing the burden on internal teams. The portal has supported the migration of more than 50,000 investor records and documents. It also connects with existing infrastructure through APIs, including CRM systems such as DealCloud and Salesforce.

To learn more or request a demonstration, visit anduintransact.com/anduin-investor-portal.

Sources indicate that anduin Transactions is the end-to-end investment management technology partner for private markets, connecting marketing, fundraising, onboarding, reporting, and ongoing servicing through one unified platform. Trusted by firms managing more than $7 trillion in aggregate AUM, Anduin has supported more than $265 billion in capital committed and over 76,000 unique investors. Visit anduintransact.com.

Industry News: Broker Action Coalition pushes for QM change on compensation cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders’ employee loan officers.
  • In a white paper recently released by BAC, the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans.
  • Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders’ employee loan officers.

In a white paper recently released by BAC, the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans.

Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026. Smaller loans are subject to graduated percentage and dollar limits.

Presently, compensation paid by a wholesale lender to an independent mortgage broker counts toward that limit, while compensation paid by a retail lender to its own employee loan officer is excluded.

The coalition argues that both types of compensation are often funded through the interest rate and are indistinguishable from the borrower’s perspective. The difference can leave brokers with less room to cover other fees that count toward the cap, potentially causing otherwise qualifying loans to exceed the limit while losing QM status and its associated liability protections.

Industry observers note that the disparity is particularly pronounced on smaller loans, where the dollar limits leave less room for additional charges. The coalition noted small-balance and rural loans are particularly vulnerable because fixed-dollar charges consume a larger share of the available cap.

The white paper also points to a decline in small-dollar mortgage lending. The share of home purchase loans under $70,000 fell from more than 11% in 2011 to less than 4% in 2020, citing research from Pew Charitable Trusts, the Urban Institute and the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

In rural and lower-cost markets, the group argues, the restrictions can make it harder for brokers to compete for loans that are already less financially attractive to originate.

In a recent development, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau‘s 2013 rulemaking established the distinction between employee and broker compensation. At the time, the bureau said including broker compensation in the calculation could help reduce the risk of mortgage brokers steering borrowers toward more expensive transactions.

The coalition acknowledges that consumer protection concern but argues that subsequent regulations addressing loan originator compensation and steering have made the points-and-fees restriction a less targeted way to address the matter.

Specifically, the group points to existing rules that prohibit loan originator compensation from varying based on a loan’s interest rate or other terms, as well as a separate prohibition on steering borrowers toward transactions that provide greater compensation.

The proposed reform would take two approaches: The primary proposal is a statutory amendment to the Truth in Lending Act that would exclude rate-funded creditor-to-broker compensation from the points-and-fees definition when it is paid under a compliant loan originator compensation agreement.

The parallel regulatory proposal would ask the CFPB to amend Regulation Z to create the same exclusion.

“The proposed reform would remove an inequitable regulatory constraint without changing the competitive forces that influence compensation today,” the paper reads. “While individual brokerages may adjust their compensation arrangements, there is little evidence to suggest that the reform would materially diminish the wholesale channel‘s overall pricing competitiveness.”.

Under the proposed language, the exclusion would apply only when compensation is funded through the interest rate, is not paid directly by the borrower or financed into the loan amount, and is established through a standing agreement between the creditor and broker that does not vary based on individual loan terms.

Sources indicate that the coalition noted the proposed requirements would prevent brokers from adjusting compensation on individual loans to circumvent the cap. The change would leave the 3% limit and existing compensation and anti-steering rules intact, with borrower-paid compensation and other fees still subject to the cap.

Recent findings suggest that data from two wholesale lenders representing $13.4 billion in combined 2026 production demonstrated that loans with 2.75% broker compensation accounted for 14.53% of units and 12.41% of volume. BAC stated the figures indicate most brokered loans close with lower compensation.

According to recent reports, the group also argued that the CFPB has authority under the Truth in Lending Act to make the change to preserve access to affordable mortgage credit. It cited the bureau’s 2019 assessment of the Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage rule, which documented fee waivers and other challenges affecting smaller brokered loans.

#6208. Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating fresh requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure.
  • According to recent reports, agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure.
  • It has been revealed that that shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:07 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Recent findings suggest that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating fresh requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

According to recent reports, agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

It has been revealed that that shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

Sources indicate that “They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane mentioned. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”.

Sources indicate that vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the tech giant has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

Cochrane said Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

“We’ve always noted that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

According to recent reports, that approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

The next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create upcoming revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

Bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

Sources indicate that vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane said the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

The goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

That distinction is becoming crucial as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

The growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

An AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

“Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane said.

It has been revealed that CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

In a recent development, another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

According to recent reports, this creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

Sources indicate that for organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

Cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

In a recent development, the distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

Recent findings suggest that “If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he said.

Industry observers note that that approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

In a recent development, for enterprises, this is an important architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

Sources indicate that inference costs can increase quickly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

According to recent reports, cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

He described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

The broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

That does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

Recent findings suggest that that moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

It has been revealed that cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

Sources indicate that cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

Sources indicate that he also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane remarked, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

Industry observers note that enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain notable, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

That creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

Sources indicate that as Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has replied to XRP holders who criticized him for selling most of his XRP with a Saturday Night Live GIF of Natalie Portman saying, "I never said I was a role model.".

According to Schwartz, his XRP holdings are down 88%, from a peak of roughly 26 million tokens to 3 million. His Bitcoin went from about 1,500 coins to one, and his Ether went from about 40,000 to six.

Sources indicate that schwartz wrote that he "really doesn't like risk." According to Schwartz, he and his wife agreed years ago to sell some of their coins every time crypto reached a new all-time high. In 2025, Schwartz sold around 2.5 million XRP and paid about $1.7 million in capital gains tax on the sale. He had received these tokens in 2020 and 2023.

According to recent reports, @hllywd22 @tchdwntommyd @WHTBOYRICKY @CryptoTaxFixer When XRP hit 10 cents, that seemed ridiculous. When ETH hit $1, that seemed ridiculous. What BTC hit $200, that seemed ridiculous.

Sources indicate that schwartz remarked that all of his sales were made under written trading plans, and a lawyer approved each initiative at least 30 days before each sale. According to Schwartz, his largest risk asset is still his stake in Ripple.

According to recent reports, schwartz also noted that he was a skeptic from the start and did not believe in the early price records of crypto. "When XRP hit 10 cents, that seemed ridiculous. When ETH hit $1, that seemed ridiculous," he wrote.

In his view, the price of XRP today depends on overall sentiment in the crypto market, and fees on the network barely move it. Schwartz allows that the token could capture some of the value of a successful ecosystem in the future, but there are no guarantees. On Monday, the price of XRP stands at $0.956.

On Nov. 16, Schwartz also posted a review of the XRPL codebase by the Qwen AI model. "I asked Qwen to rate my work on the XRPL software. It was mostly good. But this was harsh and it's not wrong," he wrote.

According to the review, the overall architecture of XRPL is good. Still, Qwen stated that some components of the code are too tightly coupled, and the migration to a newly introduced testing framework stopped halfway. The AI model also called the code generation in XRPL opaque.

Several XRPL developers replied to the post and said that they are already rewriting some of these parts of the code. Other people asked for formal verification of the XRPL core before the upcoming features planned for 2027 go live.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1508 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Sources indicate that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He stated he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

In a recent development, his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be mentioned for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan stated. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he mentioned. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she mentioned, but it showed cold.

Recent findings suggest that “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova remarked. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

It has been revealed that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova mentioned. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney remarked.

Sources indicate that she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She indicates music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he indicates, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

According to recent reports, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

It has been revealed that “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer noted. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea states she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Industry observers note that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

In a recent development, his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein noted.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share upcoming songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

Industry observers note that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Industry observers note that kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she noted.

Industry observers note that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

It has been revealed that so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova stated, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

Tech Report: Senate committee advances Matt Jones’ nomination as FHA commissioner

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote.
  • The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration.
  • Committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) noted Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote.

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration. Jones would permanently fill the vacancy left by Frank Cassidy in June and succeed Joseph Gormley, who has been serving in the role on an acting basis.

Committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) noted Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support. According to Scott, housing affordability remains one of the biggest challenges facing families across America, but if confirmed, Jones “will play an important role in implementing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and helping more families achieve the American dream of home ownership.”.

Jones presently serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing. He previously was associate vice president of government housing finance at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), senior adviser for capital markets at Amerifirst Home Mortgage, and senior counsel for the Senate’s Finance and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committees.The 13-11 vote reflected partisan divisions over the direction of federal housing policy and FHA’s role in addressing affordability and ownership gaps.

Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the committee’s ranking member, voted against the nomination, saying Jones’ office has “cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families instead of corporations.”.

“We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump administration‘s disastrous economic policies,” Warren stated. If confirmed, Jones would oversee FHA’s single-family, multifamily and health care mortgage insurance portfolios. FHA at the moment insures roughly $2 trillion in mortgages.

The FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels. The results have renewed industry pressure on FHA to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums to ease costs for first-time and lower-income borrowers.

Jones would also inherit an agency that has seen a series of policy adjustments under HUD Secretary Scott Turner, including efforts to revise servicing standards and modernize technology infrastructure.

MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit noted the trade group supports the nomination due to Jones’ “extensive mortgage industry experience, deep understanding of government housing finance, and leadership of FHA’s single-family operations.”.

“We urge the full Senate to confirm Matt Jones before the 119th Congress adjourns and look forward to working with him and HUD to continue modernizing FHA programs and to improve affordability for owning and renting a home,” Broeksmit mentioned.

Sources indicate that XRP printed a 7% price recovery in yesterday's trading session, which barely helps the price, considering its long-term market performance. Given the volume we are witnessing on the market, there is barely any traction out there.

Sources indicate that the bounce started from $0.894, and at press time XRP is trading at $0.948. The recovery candle came on lower volume than the red one before it.

Recent findings suggest that since early November, XRP has lost roughly 30% of its value and given up everything it built throughout the August rally. In October, the 200 EMA acted as a strong resistance that XRP was unable to break.

Recent findings suggest that the main problem here is the lack of bullish narratives on the market. Bitcoin lost almost 15% of its value in the blink of an eye, without any solid catalysts or news, apart from ones that have been around for months now: AI, the Nvidia crash, the Anthropic IPO and cybersecurity risks. On November 15, BTC touched a four-month low around $62,000.

Investors aren't buying XRP en masse either. US-listed XRP ETFs saw $19.13 million in net outflows in the week through November 13, the heaviest weekly redemption since March.

The possibility of a recovery is real, but it is minuscule. The RSI dipped below 25 before the bounce, so part of yesterday's move is simply a reaction to the oversold market. There are little to no fundamental factors that can help XRP stay above key levels for longer than a day or two.

Whether buyers can reclaim the $1 level or not is the main test for XRP this week. A short-lived price bounce here won't change the situation as a whole, unfortunately.

#6201. Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (586 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions.
  • 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte, the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan.
  • The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions.

Sources indicate that in a Nov. 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte, the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan. 4, 2027, to Jan. 4, 2028.

The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income.

The letter was signed by the Community Associations Institute, Community Association Roundtable, Community Home Lenders of America (CHLA), Housing Policy Council and National Association of Mortgage Brokers (NAMB).

The groups said they support adequately funded condominium reserves but argued that associations, lenders and homeowners need more time to prepare for the change.

Some have asked for change before. In June, NAMB asked the FHFA to delay upcoming Fannie and Freddie condo review and insurance standards by 12 months. But Fannie Mae retired its limited review process for condominium projects on Aug. 3.

“Condominium project eligibility has already declined following recent changes to project review requirements, including the elimination of Limited Review options,” the groups wrote.

The coalition identified three primary concerns with the planned increase, stating that “the change could have unintended consequences for condominium financing and housing availability.”.

First, many condominium associations operate on annual budget cycles and cannot easily adjust their funding midyear. Some may also need updated reserve studies, board approvals or homeowner consultations before changing their funding practices.

The groups also noted questions remain about how the newly introduced requirement will apply to existing budgets, recently completed reserve studies, major capital improvement projects and alternative funding arrangements.

Lenders, servicers and condo management companies will also need time to revision their systems, underwriting procedures and project reviews.

Second, the groups warned that associations unable to meet the higher reserve requirement or qualify under an alternative reserve study provision could lose eligibility for conventional financing through the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). The groups raised concerns that this could reduce the pool of potential buyers, make it more difficult for existing homeowners to sell or refinance, and put pressure on condo resale values.

The impact could be particularly pronounced in older buildings, smaller communities and associations with more “modest-income” homeowners, the letter stated. Projects that lose conventional financing eligibility could become more reliant on nonagency or portfolio loans, which may be more expensive or less readily available.

Lastly, the coalition stated higher reserve contributions could add to housing costs at a time when homeowners are already facing elevated mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance premiums, maintenance expenses and association fees.

It has been revealed that fannie Mae has estimated that the higher reserve requirement could add an average of $13 to $14 per month to condominium owners’ costs, but the actual increase would vary by association, according to the coalition. Its accompanying analysis illustrated how the additional five percentage points could affect homeowners if the entire increase were funded through regular assessments.

As part of the proposed one-year extension, the coalition urged FHFA to convene industry stakeholders to evaluate the financial and operational effects of the change, clarify how existing reserve studies and funding arrangements will be treated, and develop transition provisions for associations working toward adequate reserve funding.

“We believe that strengthening condominium financial health and maintaining housing affordability should be complementary objectives,” the letter said.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

According to recent reports, why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

XRP Ledger Foundation Director of Community Hussein Zangana (Vet) shared a tidbit of XRPL's early history in a recent X post.

Vet noted that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) still carries traces of Satoshi Nakamoto’s original Bitcoin design, highlighting two features.

It has been revealed that in 2011, three engineers—David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto—began developing the XRP Ledger (XRPL). Fascinated by Bitcoin, they set out to create a better version that improved upon its limitations—with the goal of creating a digital asset that was more sustainable and built specifically for payments.

As reported, the first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written by David Schwartz, who is Ripple CTO emeritus, about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011.

In a recent development, vet delves into the earliest part of XRP Ledger history, noting that 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, wrote. Vet added that Jed McCaleb also copied Satoshi’s timekeeping code into the XRPL, even including one of the Bitcoin creator’s comments shared as a screenshot.

Did you know all of us on the XRP Ledger use design choices by Satoshi daily? 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Satoshi wrote. Jed copied Satoshi's timekeeping code into the XRPL, including one of Satoshi's comments. By the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone. In December 2014, Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment. Two design choices of Satoshi still remain on the XRPL and all of us use at least one of it. Signature curve secp256k1 (we also support Ed25519 thus not everyone uses this) and how XRPL addresses are generated from the public key with SHA-256 followed by RIPEMD-160, that's what all of us use.

The quote "Never go to sea with two chronometers; take one or three" is a classic maritime adage famously included by Satoshi Nakamoto (the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin) within the Bitcoin source code.

Vet explained that by the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone from the XRP Ledger. In December 2014, former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment.

However, two of Satoshi's design choices still remain on the XRP Ledger: the first is the secp256k1 signature curve, which Bitcoin uses and which the XRP Ledger continues to support. However, the ledger also supports Ed25519, meaning not every XRPL user relies on secp256k1.

"I remember David saying they used secp256k1 so no one would doubt the security because it's the same as Bitcoin's, etc.," Vet stated, citing the insight of the Ripple CTO emeritus on secp256k1, adding, "Lots of interesting things to dig into from the early days.".

The second is the method used to generate XRP Ledger addresses from public keys. The process applies SHA-256 hashing followed by RIPEMD-160, a design inherited from Bitcoin that remains common to all XRPL addresses.

Asked why the timekeeping code and Satoshi's comment were removed, Vet explained that this became leftover code as upcoming code was introduced, so it was cleaned up.

Medical AI startup Boltz raises $110M to speed up small molecule research

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.
  • In a recent development, bessemer led the Series A investment.
  • Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:17 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.

In a recent development, bessemer led the Series A investment. Boltz stated on Wednesday that the fund was joined by a large group of upcoming and returning backers. The consortium included Greycroft, Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and others.

Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it. As a result, researchers start drug discovery projects by looking for molecules that have a high binding affinity with pathogens. They often review hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules per project. The process can take months and often costs millions of dollars.

In a recent development, boltz offers an AI model called BoltzMol-1 that speeds up the workflow. It generates binding affinity data by reviewing only a few dozen, particularly promising molecules instead of the hundreds of thousands usually needed. The fewer molecules need to be studied, the less time the analysis takes.

According to recent reports, binding affinity evaluations don’t yield drug discoveries right away. Instead, they produce data points called small molecule hits. Those are essentially faint clues that help researchers pinpoint the area where they should focus their efforts.

Boltz staffers asked BoltzMol-1 to look for small molecule hits across 10 “challenging and therapeutically-relevant targets.” Targets are biological building blocks that play a role in disease processes. According to the company, the model found small molecule hits for six of the targets.

Scientists can adapt BoltzMol-1 to project-specific constraints. If a research team has access to a relatively limited number of compounds, it could configure the model to only consider small molecules that can be made from those compounds. When material procurement is not an obstacle, BoltzMol-1 evaluates a much larger number of candidates.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer also offers a second model called BoltzProt-1. It can generate tens of thousands of protein designs based on data gleaned from small molecule hits. Additionally, BoltzProt-1 automatically reviews each protein to determine if it could be used to develop a newly introduced drug.

It has been revealed that usually, AI models evaluate protein designs based on rubrics that provide only an indirect view of their effectiveness. BoltzProt-1 uses more direct metrics. The company claims that BoltzProt-1’s protein evaluation mechanism demonstrated “higher success” than several competing models during internal tests.

According to recent reports, boltz sells its algorithms via an application programming interface that is billed based on token usage. According to the company, customers’ token consumption has grown by a factor of 50 since BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 rolled out in June. Boltz counts six of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies as clients.

Industry observers note that the organization will use its new funding to grow its headcount and procure more computing infrastructure. The extra hardware should make it easier for Boltz to keep up with leading AI labs such as newly public Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group. Over the past year, both companies have introduced models that are highly adapted to biology research tasks.

It has been revealed that boltz has already started training a new generation of molecule design algorithms. The company says that they are “showing substantial improvements” over its current models.

#6196. Why some regional brokerages are avoiding ancillary services

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1405 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Why some regional brokerages are avoiding ancillary services

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • housing market may see fewer than 4 million existing home sales in 2027.
  • Recent findings suggest that from newly introduced mortgage joint ventures to diving into mortgage servicing, companies from eXp Realty to HomeServices of America are looking to further integrate the disparate parts of a real estate transaction into one vertical platform.
  • Industry observers note that “Our company has been around for 153 years and our strategy has always been to be masters of our craft and not to chase every adjacent revenue stream,” Matt Leone, the chief marketing officer at Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no secret that the U.S. housing market may see fewer than 4 million existing home sales in 2027. In an attempt to boost ever-tightening margins and claim a larger slice of the transaction pie, many large national brokerages have spent the past year doubling down on ancillary services.

Recent findings suggest that from newly introduced mortgage joint ventures to diving into mortgage servicing, companies from eXp Realty to HomeServices of America are looking to further integrate the disparate parts of a real estate transaction into one vertical platform. While this may be the way some of the nation’s largest brokerage companies are thinking about the future, many regional brokerages with strong market share in their states or metros are taking a different tack.

Industry observers note that “Our company has been around for 153 years and our strategy has always been to be masters of our craft and not to chase every adjacent revenue stream,” Matt Leone, the chief marketing officer at Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, remarked. “I think that we are a residential resale, latest development and property management brokerage. Mortgage and title may offer additional income, but our greatest opportunity is to stay relentlessly focused on real estate and be the best at that. I think, when you venture into other arenas, your core gets saturated and your eyes come off the prize.”.

Like BHS, Linda O’Koniewski’s RealTrends Verified firm, Leading Edge Real Estate, is also staying out of ancillary services.

Recent findings suggest that “While margins are critically thin for brokerages, and the income would be welcome, we have given it all up,” O’Koniewski remarked, noting that her firm had previously had partnerships with insurance and mortgage companies. “What our clients need is the best loan officer and product. They need a super-responsive insurance agent. We are dedicating ourselves to developing processes and strategies that pre-resolve preventable problems in a transaction and create the best outcomes for our clients.”.

O’Koniewski added that her firm’s in-house legal counsel has also suggested homing in on real estate as industries like mortgage and title are not their primary area of expertise.

Although firms like Leading Edge and BHS may not own or have ancillary services joint ventures, this doesn’t mean they lack relationships with lenders or title companies.

At BHS, instead of offering mortgage or title services directly or through a joint venture, the manufacturer works with trusted mortgage or title professionals to contribute to the company’s blog, sponsor its podcasts and participate in educational panel discussions.

Leone said BHS works to establish relationships with the top mortgage and title professionals through a “massive in-house commitment to marketing and content creation,” bringing voices from ancillary services industries that BHS feels are the most aligned with its culture and mission.

Sources indicate that “They’re providing their expertise to our audience that follows us, as well as providing advertising support to expand the audience that views our 18-plus podcasts and in-house created episodic series shows,” he mentioned. “It is legitimate advertising and earned media exposure at fair market value that allows us to get their expertise to broadcast that to our client base and it also allows us to have an ancillary source of legitimate income.”.

Through these posts and marketing material, Leone mentioned BHS is looking to educate its agents and clients, which is why the brokerage likes to partner with creative and experienced ancillary services providers through the program.

“We’re bringing experienced professionals that have seen it all before, and we like to bring those individuals in to get their insights,” Leone said. “Hopefully it allows everyone to stay informed and that is our goal when we’re creating content.”.

While not yet as advanced as BHS’s marketing machine, this is what Peter Voss is looking to do with the in-house video production and editing segment he and his team have released at 3% Listing Co.

Industry observers note that “Agents can schedule a time with the in-house video team whenever they want and work with our director on a script and then get in front of the camera and record. We take care of all the editing and produce the video,” Voss said.

Voss said, for his firm, the video production started as a way to provide services to their agents that are beneficial to their business, but also something his firm could afford without significantly increasing overhead costs.

“It is a way to help our agents get their branding out and hopefully generate more transactions, which helps them but also helps our business,” he stated.

In the future, Voss said they are looking to expand this service beyond just 3% Listing Co agents, allowing the tech giant to have an additional revenue stream similar to BHS’s operation.

While brokerages like BHS, 3% Listing Co. and Leading Edge may not feel the need to go all-in on ancillary services, Michele Harrington, at First Team Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified firm, sees them as a must-have.

According to recent reports, “It is kind of a no-brainer. The profit margins in the real estate brokerage business are just so tiny, so any little bump in the market or a downturn in the market is really going to hurt,” Harrington, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, remarked.

In a recent development, this is why Harrington believes anyone who owns a brokerage should be exploring ancillary services. Even prior to opening First Team, Harrington, who previously led a 300-agent company based in Southern California, had her own escrow and mortgage companies.

At First Team, Harrington runs an escrow firm and a mortgage brokerage operation. She previously had mortgage joint ventures, but said she preferred going the owned mortgage operation route in order to maximize margins.

“The joint venture business isn’t my favorite type of mortgage operation because it is hard to be competitive and have good rates for consumers when everyone involved is trying to make a profit,” she said. “So, your best bet is being a broker where you can go directly to the banks or Rocket or United Wholesale Mortgage and broker the loan. It makes you way more competitive.”.

By owning ancillary services, not only can you boost your profit margins, Harrington also feels it enables brokers to provide even better service to consumers.

In a recent development, “It gives you more control. If something goes wrong with escrow or mortgage, the agent calls me, and I tell the president that they need to fix it. That level of control is a nice perk for the agents,” Harrington stated.

Beyond providing her agents with more control over transactions, Harrington noted having ancillary businesses within her company also helps First Team be more competitive as a brokerage.

“If I want to be more competitive in my splits or be more competitive by offering signing bonuses, I can do those things because ancillary services increase my margins,” she noted.

While Voss sees the value of having ancillary services operations, especially when it comes to revenue opportunities, he still doesn’t believe the juice is necessarily worth the squeeze.

Sources indicate that “We have talked about bringing mortgage in-house, but what we have found is that in-house operations can be a turn off to a lot of agents,” Voss remarked. “They feel like it is kind of forced on them to have to send their clients to their firm’s mortgage lender. We are really focused on recruitment right now, so that is why we have shied away from this.”.

Leone agrees, telling HousingWire that in-house mortgage or title operations often feel like a “forced option” that agents have to suggest to their clients.

“We don’t want to get in between the relationship of the client and our agent and the agents understand who is best for their client and who is best for that transaction,” he said. “Different lenders make sense for different neighborhoods, price points and scenarios and we don’t want to get in the middle of that.”.

Instead Leone and Voss feel that their companies can generate more revenue by focusing on being the best at helping buyers and sellers transact real estate.

“We really focus on our relationships with mortgage lenders and title companies and making sure that we make their jobs easier so that they may be more open to sending business to us and our agents because they know we will get the job done,” Voss stated.

Tech Report: Cardano Holders Put Billions of ADA Coins to Block $5 Million Copper Reserve

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve.".
  • According to recent reports, the vote closed on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve.".

According to recent reports, the vote closed on Nov. 15, and DReps holding 2.86 billion ADA voted against the proposal, according to Cardano governance data. DReps with 20.02 million ADA voted in favor of it.

DRep John MacPherson was among those who voted "No," and he explained his decision in a post on X.

Recent findings suggest that macPherson wrote that he is not against real-world assets on Cardano. Still, he remarked the proposal asks the treasury "to take on both the copper price and the ada price," and Toto Finance would collect "up to about 3.4M ada in fees.".

At the same time, MacPherson remarked that the proposal is “more honest about its risks than most.”.

Industry observers note that toto Finance, a firm led by Monty Metzger, submitted the proposal on Oct. 15. ADA is trading at $0.152 on Monday, and the requested 22 million ADA is now worth around $3.3 million.

Recent findings suggest that the blueprint was to buy copper with 14.72 million ADA and store it in a warehouse near Upcoming Orleans. Toto Finance wanted to issue one CuTT token for each pound of copper. The metal would be sold in 18 to 24 months.

The Cardano Foundation, which votes as a DRep, declared its "No" vote in October.

"We recognize the opportunity in real-world asset tokenization; however, this proposal places 22,000,000 ada under the recipient's sole control to fund a fee-heavy concentrated commodity position whose safeguards are not yet in place," the foundation wrote.

Three members of the Constitutional Committee voted "No," and the other four members did not vote.

Crypto commentator Ingeniero Cripto agreed with MacPherson in the replies under his post. He called the "double exposure" to the prices of copper and ADA the key problem of the proposal, as the Cardano treasury already holds ADA.

According to him, RWAs on Cardano make sense, but “funding the asset itself is a different question than funding the rails.”.

#6194. Tech Report: NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (823 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • It has been revealed that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • It has been revealed that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

It has been revealed that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents remarked.

It has been revealed that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO stated he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

According to recent reports, pierpoint noted he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or proposal.”.

According to recent reports, pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also stated the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Recent findings suggest that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Industry observers note that pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears noted the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” mentioned David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Sources indicate that pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

It has been revealed that “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

Could GTA 6 be stealing retail’s attention just as digital asset markets struggle to bring individual investors back?

The scale of the launch is hard to ignore. Reports put GTA 6 pre-orders at well over 10 million copies before its worldwide release. The game also carries expectations of $1.85 billion in revenue during its first three days.

According to recent reports, workers are making room for it, too. BambooHR data showed time-off requests for launch day running 9% to 17% above a typical third Thursday of November. A separate Zety survey found 22% of Gen Z workers planned around the release.

It has been revealed that that is a sizeable chunk of the demographic that crypto platforms have spent years trying to attract. Gaming and crypto compete for the same online attention, particularly among younger audiences who spend hours on streaming platforms, social media and digital communities.

For us, checking Bitcoin prices, chasing the latest meme coin and following market-moving posts can easily become part of the daily routine. But GTA 6 offers something considerably more entertaining than watching another sideways trading session.

The launch is also driving enormous engagement across YouTube and Reddit. Sensor Tower estimates point to more than 50 million additional visits to food delivery and restaurant apps in the US over 30 days.

Crypto’s social media ecosystem could find itself competing for a much smaller share of that attention.

It has been revealed that there is another reason the timing is interesting. Retail crypto trading has been weakening even as the broader market has attracted fresh capital.

Recent findings suggest that eToro clients placed 62% fewer crypto trades in October than a year earlier. Robinhood’s crypto trading volume also fell 48% year over year in October, while Coinbase consumer spot volume dropped 59%.

The figures show that rising market valuations have not translated into the same level of retail trading activity seen during previous cycles.

This leaves crypto exposed to competition for speculative attention. Institutional investors can continue trading through market cycles, but retail often depends on excitement, momentum, and whatever narrative is dominating the internet.

But GTA 6 has all three. The game could temporarily pull casual traders away from exchanges, particularly those who spend their evenings chasing small-cap tokens and following crypto KOLs. Meme coins could be especially vulnerable if their usual audience spends the next several days exploring Vice City instead.

According to recent reports, there is also an ironic possibility that GTA 6 could create fresh opportunities for crypto speculation. Gaming-themed tokens and GTA-related meme coins could attract traders looking to profit from the launch itself.

Industry observers note that bitcoin does not need gamers watching charts every minute to keep trading. But an industry built around speculation, online communities, and retail enthusiasm cannot afford to ignore where that attention goes.
