Newly introduced CEO at Villa eyes manufactured housing, ADU opportunity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Offsite construction, one of the housing affordability crisis’s hidden-in-plain-sight solutions, gained a blast of momentum this summer when the ROAD Act called for removing the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes.
  • Villa, which operates in California and Colorado, is among them.
  • Since launching in 2019, the company has delivered more than 425 homes across three core verticals: manufactured single-family communities, ADUs on single-family lots, and ADUs within multifamily communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Offsite construction, one of the housing affordability crisis’s hidden-in-plain-sight solutions, gained a blast of momentum this summer when the ROAD Act called for removing the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes. Now, some builders are preparing to capitalize on that growing buzz.

Villa, which operates in California and Colorado, is among them.

Since launching in 2019, the company has delivered more than 425 homes across three core verticals: manufactured single-family communities, ADUs on single-family lots, and ADUs within multifamily communities.

The builder originally focused exclusively on ADUs, but has since expanded into primary homes, delivering its first batch of manufactured single-family houses in Northern California earlier this year. The organization is currently building 25 homes in Santa Rosa, California and 14 duplexes in Westminster, Colorado, while also helping rebuild housing for victims of the 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena, California.

Recent findings suggest that the goal now is to scale both the ADU and manufactured housing businesses, with looks for larger single-family communities of up to about 100 lots. To support that growth, Villa confirmed earlier this week that it hired David Messenger, former CFO of Century Communities, as its next CEO.

According to recent reports, for Messenger, moving from one of the country’s largest production homebuilders to an offsite builder focused on ADUs and infill development is quite a pivot. But it also represents an opportunity to focus more on attainable housing in the high-cost areas where Villa operates.

For example, in Santa Rosa, a city of about 180,000 north of San Francisco, the average home price is about $705,000. Comparatively, homes in Villa’s upcoming community, Acacia Village, start at $620,000.

“I’ve been drawn to affordable, attainable housing. I think it’s something that the country needs,” Messenger stated in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Beyond the opportunity to deliver attainable housing where it’s badly needed, Messenger sees room for growth across all of Villa’s verticals.

In a recent development, “We’ve got three verticals already established. I think all three can continue to grow,” he noted.

Villa’s ADU business has plenty of room to grow, Messenger stated. Homeowners in California and Colorado are driving strong and growing demand, while California multifamily operators are increasingly building ADUs on open or underutilized land to generate extra rental income.

“More and more multifamily operators see [ADUs] as a way to increase their rental income…at a relatively low cost to their overall project,” Messenger said.

According to recent reports, the other growth opportunity is in Villa’s newly introduced manufactured home communities. Messenger sees an opening to partner with land developers to build larger communities, potentially with up to around 100 lots. Instead of taking on the expense and risk of acquiring, entitling and developing land themselves, Villa plans to purchase fully entitled and developed land.

“There is an opportunity to work with land developers who, as they’re developing land, are looking for a takeout. The land developers don’t necessarily want to own the land long term. I think if we can provide them a takeout when it’s finished, that is an attractive option for both of us, as we can buy a finished lot. I don’t think that Villa is going to be in the game of developing land, and we’re not looking to take on entitlement risk,” Messenger explained.

Industry observers note that messenger also plans to draw on his experience at Century Communities to help Villa build a more scalable operation. Although the companies operate differently, he believes many of the same production homebuilding principles can apply.

Sources indicate that “Having spent 10 years at a production homebuilder, you learn how to establish repeatable processes. Homebuilding involves unpredictable complications every day, so the goal is to make those issues more predictable. Offsite construction lends itself to that because a significant portion of the home is built in a factory, making the process more predictable. It’s about establishing standardized processes that can be repeated for every unit and every lot,” Messenger mentioned.

“Once we get those processes working like a machine, that’s what makes the business scalable,” he added.

As Villa scales, Messenger doesn’t expect production capacity to be an glitch. Instead of owning and operating its own factories, the company contracts with reputable, third-party production facilities to build its homes and ADUs.

“We’ve partnered with different factories all over the state of California. We partner with factories in Colorado, Nebraska and Albuquerque for dealing with those projects. We are developing an extensive array of relationships to make sure that we don’t get hamstrung by a capacity problem,” he remarked.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law in July, included a provision that removed the decades-long requirement that manufactured homes be built with a permanent steel chassis. The change has received a lot of attention, leading The Latest York Times to name chassis as its word of the day on November 11.

It has been revealed that manufacturers cite two main benefits of this rule change, which the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is now finalizing. First, removing the steel chassis gives manufactured homebuilders greater design flexibility, allowing them to build larger, multi-story and more aesthetically appealing homes that more closely resemble traditional site-built housing.

Recent findings suggest that “If you actually walk through a manufactured home product today and look at the finishes being delivered, it’s a completely different product from what people actually think about. If we can do some marketing and outreach and get people in the door to see what these homes look like, I think they’ll be amazed at what they see,” Messenger noted.

That added design flexibility could help the industry shed longstanding stigmas and gain acceptance in communities where zoning restrictions historically thwarted manufactured housing, which is typically a more affordable alternative to traditional stick-built homes.

Manufacturers also see an opportunity to expand into high-cost urban and suburban infill markets, where multi-story designs can make higher-density development more economically feasible. Villa, which operates in high-cost cities with limited developable land, is among the homebuilders positioned to benefit from this rule change.

According to recent reports, “As we’re evaluating communities, not having a chassis requirement should open up more lots and communities where we can build on,” Messenger remarked. “I think it provides additional opportunities for us.”.

Binance’s Co-Founder States Crypto Market Pullback Is Temporary

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (298 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yi He, the co-founder of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has sparked discussions across the crypto market after urging retail traders to stay calm even as major crypto assets continue to post massive daily losses.
  • Yi He’s consoling statement has come as crypto traders grow increasingly weary and the prolonged market volatility begins to cause even bigger losses, with Bitcoin retesting $63,000.
  • In her post, Yi urged investors holding major crypto assets that have been substantially affected by the severe market volatility to remain calm amid the latest market downturn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yi He, the co-founder of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has sparked discussions across the crypto market after urging retail traders to stay calm even as major crypto assets continue to post massive daily losses.

Yi He’s consoling statement has come as crypto traders grow increasingly weary and the prolonged market volatility begins to cause even bigger losses, with Bitcoin retesting $63,000.

In her post, Yi urged investors holding major crypto assets that have been substantially affected by the severe market volatility to remain calm amid the latest market downturn.

She described the ongoing crypto market pullback as ‘temporary’ while assuring spot traders that they have little reason to worry.

Alongside the post, Yi He shared a link to the Binance app showcasing a 30-day asset change of approximately -$101.31 million in her account.

The figure indicates the amount of losses the pro-crypto investor has suffered on her holdings over a period of about a month, from October 17 to November 16, 2026.

Although the showcased portfolio shows a decline in the founder’s holdings, it does not establish whether the decline represents realized trading losses, unrealized losses, withdrawals, or other changes in Yi He’s account.

It appears that some investors may have found comfort in Yi He's message as they expressed support, noting that turbulent conditions like these don’t necessarily last long.

However, other commentators have questioned whether wealthy industry figures like Yi He can fully understand the financial pressure facing retail traders at a time like this.

Some of the arguments questioned how meaningful such reassurance could be for retail investors, arguing that losing 100 million yuan might not significantly affect someone with substantial wealth like her.

Meanwhile, a loss of 20,000 or 30,000 yuan could wipe out an ordinary investor's savings.

#6189. Latest Update: Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of what it paid

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (870 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of what it paid

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Financial software company Intuit Inc.
  • Coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the manufacturer paid.
  • According to recent reports, although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:17 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Financial software company Intuit Inc. today revealed that it has agreed to sell its Mailchimp email marketing business to Italian technology holding company Bending Spoons S.p.A. for about $3.68 billion.

Coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the manufacturer paid. The 2021 purchase was the largest in Intuit’s history at the time.

According to recent reports, although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares. That leaves Intuit with $3.31 billion in cash from the sale, according to the companies. Included in the deal is The Rocket Science Group LLC, the legal entity behind Mailchimp. Closing is expected in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

Selling Mailchimp is stated to sharpen Intuit’s focus on the artificial intelligence-native tools it has built to help businesses win latest customers, manage their pipeline and grow. Once the deal closes, Intuit intends to use the cash proceeds to buy back its own shares before the end of fiscal 2027.

Jack Tam, a senior vice president at Intuit, said the company is confident Bending Spoons “will lead Mailchimp to continued success in this next chapter.”.

Growth at Mailchimp has stalled in recent quarters. Revenue from the business fell 1% to $313 million in the quarter ended Oct. 31. Intuit’s full-year guidance has Mailchimp revenue coming in flat to down 1%. In November 2024, Chief Financial Officer Sandeep Aujla told analysts that Intuit was seeing higher churn from smaller Mailchimp customers.

In a recent development, “Mailchimp is a powerful brand, built over two decades of reshaping the email marketing category and redefining how companies grow their audiences,” said Luca Ferrari, co-founder and chief executive of Bending Spoons. “We’re honored to welcome it to Bending Spoons and excited about what we can accomplish together.”.

Ferrari added that Bending Spoons prepares to invest substantially in Mailchimp after closing. According to Bending Spoons, the transformation of a business it acquires is typically deep, entailing reorganized teams, overhauled technology and redesigned user interfaces.

It has been revealed that founded in 2013, Bending Spoons has built a portfolio of digital businesses that includes AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Tractive, Vimeo and WeTransfer. Since listing on the Nasdaq in July, the firm has also completed acquisitions of Airtable Inc. for $1.285 billion and whiteboard platform Miro for $1.355 billion.

Industry observers note that intuit declared the sale alongside its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results. For the quarter, it reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.91, up 56% from $1.87 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $4.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting adjusted earnings of $2.70 per share on revenue of $4.31 billion.

In a recent development, for its fiscal second quarter, Intuit expects adjusted earnings per share of $3.17 to $3.22 on revenue of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion. Intuit lowered its full-year revenue guidance to between $23.08 billion and $23.37 billion.

Industry observers note that behind the cut is Credit Karma, the company’s personal finance and credit score service, which is now forecast to grow 3% to 7% this fiscal year, down from 11% to 13% previously. Intuit reiterated its full-year adjusted earnings guidance of $22.88 to $23.12 per share. None of the guidance includes the effect of the Mailchimp sale.

Intuit shares fell more than 10% in after-hours trading.

#6188. Rate’s Jesse Allen: Reverse mortgage lenders should strategy for the ‘down case,’ not FHA relief

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (906 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Rate’s Jesse Allen: Reverse mortgage lenders should strategy for the ‘down case,’ not FHA relief

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With mortgage lenders continuing to cut expenses, including personnel, as the originations forecast for 2027 dims, Jesse Allen noted the reverse mortgage business at Rate is still growing and he isn’t waiting for federal housing leaders to offer help.
  • At last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association Annual Meeting & Expo, Allen mentioned he’s planning for the “down case” on Federal Housing Administration policy regarding upfront mortgage insurance premiums (MIP) for Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs).
  • “In an uncertain environment, you have to plan and execute to your down case scenarios, and then when something better than down case happens, you’re that much better,” Allen remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With mortgage lenders continuing to cut expenses, including personnel, as the originations forecast for 2027 dims, Jesse Allen noted the reverse mortgage business at Rate is still growing and he isn’t waiting for federal housing leaders to offer help.

At last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association Annual Meeting & Expo, Allen mentioned he’s planning for the “down case” on Federal Housing Administration policy regarding upfront mortgage insurance premiums (MIP) for Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs). Allen’s comments came not long after Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley said the Trump administration is “very comfortable” with current MIP structures for FHA-insured single-family home loans and reverse mortgages.

“In an uncertain environment, you have to plan and execute to your down case scenarios, and then when something better than down case happens, you’re that much better,” Allen remarked.

It has been revealed that allen, the president of the 55+ lending division at Rate and a NRMLA board member for 2026-27, sat down with HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily at NRMLA Annual to discuss some of the hot topics of interest for industry professionals. He mentioned that lenders should look to expand their product menus to insulate themselves from any obstacles to federally insured loans, and he pitched responsible home equity release as the next significant opportunity for the wider mortgage industry.

In a recent development, NRMLA and other trade groups have spent the past year arguing that the FHA could lower the upfront mortgage insurance premium for certain borrowers. Allen said that cutting some fees would pull more people into the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, which he called “basic insurance economics.” NRMLA has also laid out the math to lower premiums for borrowers who utilize less of their HECM proceeds while lobbying to eliminate second appraisals.

But with the political transition underway after the recent midterm elections, Allen does not expect quick action. “I’m not building my business model or business case around that,” he said. “If positive things happen, it’s wind in the sails.”.

Still, a lower upfront MIP could be “powerful for older homeowners” who want to access their equity responsibly, he stated, as they might tap 30% to 40% of their available line of credit now while saving the rest for later in retirement.

Sources indicate that when asked whether he thinks a more balanced Congress is coming in 2027, Allen said everyone’s definition of balanced differs. But he also believes that if Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) takes over the Senate banking committee, “we’re going to see more regulatory interest.” Allen’s approach, he added, is to operate daily as though auditors are showing up, which should be the standard for a business that serves a protected class of senior homeowners.

Industry observers note that allen clarified that Rate is a nondelegated correspondent lender for proprietary reverse mortgage products and is fully delegated on FHA-backed HECM products. Proprietary loans make up about 40% of Rate’s reverse mortgage originations, he said, and he estimated them at 55% to 65% of its volume based on their typically larger loan sizes.

Similar to the industry at large, private-label loans are where growth is happening at Rate, although its HECM volume is rising too, Allen mentioned, with the company outpacing the industry year over year. According to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight, Rate was the 13th-largest HECM lender in the country through the first nine months of the year, with its 228 endorsements up 41% compared to the same period in 2025.

Sources indicate that proprietary loans often serve borrowers that FHA products can’t, including owners of high-value homes and those who want to pay off consumer debt without it counting against them in qualification — a guideline NRMLA has pushed to change. But Allen mentioned his team spends time reminding loan officers that the HECM is “still an awesome product.”.

Compared with a traditional home equity line of credit, he said, a HECM line of credit mitigates the risk that falling home values lead to frozen lines, leaving borrowers without access when “they need their equity the most.” HECM lines of credit can grow for the life of the loan if the borrower doesn’t exhaust funds and meets requirements like property tax and insurance payments. Proprietary lines of credit typically stop growing after seven to 10 years, Allen added.

Allen pointed to reverse for purchase financing as a tool for addressing affordability. He remarked that one of Rate’s top loan officers recently closed a reverse for purchase for the parent of one of his real estate agent partners. The LO had a couple of reverse mortgages under his belt but had never done a purchase deal, and he worked with one of the company’s specialists to get it done.

“Specialty lending in general is a massive priority for most mortgage companies today,” Allen said, naming non-QM and builder programs alongside reverse.

Allen thinks that today’s retirees are less willing to sacrifice their lifestyles. Reverse mortgage proceeds can fund a variety of uses — from family vacations to in-home care that eases the load on adult children, or even a move into a 55-plus community without draining savings.

“That’s why I love this business, because it’s infinitely customizable,” he mentioned. “Every client is unique, every situation is unique, and we have this expanding suite of products to really help deliver for the clients … so that they can get the joy out of the transaction.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was announced on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation noted.

Recent findings suggest that solana released on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status.".

In a recent development, the Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

"For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

According to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

Recent findings suggest that firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation remarked.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

"A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once.".

It has been revealed that earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

#6184. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1160 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.
  • In a recent development, the world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy.
  • A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.

In a recent development, the world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

Sources indicate that the window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”.

The data flywheel. Early owners generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

Industry observers note that the data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

It has been revealed that momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Recent findings suggest that fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

According to recent reports, jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its major commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

Industry observers note that at AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”.

According to recent reports, finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook indicates Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”.

According to recent reports, prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”.

According to recent reports, swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

According to recent reports, farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

In a recent development, A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”.

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one significant shot once you have it.

According to recent reports, chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one states, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#6183. Industry News: Texas’ population boom is opening doors for new real estate agents

Industry News: Texas’ population boom is opening doors for new real estate agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that few states are changing as quickly as Texas.
  • Texas’ population has passed 31 million, and the suburbs surrounding Dallas, Houston, Austin and San Antonio are stretching farther and farther out.
  • Sources indicate that expensive markets with little buildable land work differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that few states are changing as quickly as Texas. It added more people than any other state between 2024 and 2025, and builders there got the green light for more fresh homes in 2025 than anywhere else in the country. More people and more houses mean more deals to be done, and more room for new agents to get in on them.

Texas’ population has passed 31 million, and the suburbs surrounding Dallas, Houston, Austin and San Antonio are stretching farther and farther out. Competition has cooled compared with the pandemic boom, yet the demand behind the market continues to climb.

Sources indicate that expensive markets with little buildable land work differently. In Texas, the business depends on sheer size, people relocating and a pipeline of newly built homes.

Recent findings suggest that over the 12 months ending July 2025, Texas grew by 391,243 people, a bigger gain than any other state posted. The population now sits near 31.7 million, 8.8% higher than in 2020.

It has been revealed that each newcomer is a future tenant, homebuyer or seller, and many will start households of their own. That means agents don’t have to count on climbing prices for opportunity. The bigger driver is people relocating and settling in for the long haul.

Raw population counts miss how often Texans relocate. In 2024, the state accounted for 7.8% of every move between states, a share topped only by Florida. Meanwhile, 3.4 million residents changed addresses without leaving Texas, the highest in-state figure in the nation.

It has been revealed that more newcomers still come from California than from anywhere else. Once all the arrivals and departures between states are netted out, Texas came out roughly 73,000 residents ahead.

All that activity is what keeps agents busy. A client arriving from out of state and one moving a few miles away both need help, which gives relocation-focused agents a reliable stream of business in and around the big metros.

It has been revealed that look at every U.S. city with 20,000 or more residents, and the five growing fastest are all in Texas. Fulshear, outside Houston, is the only one that isn’t in the Dallas-Fort Worth orbit.

Industry observers note that austin hit 1 million residents that same year, becoming the fifth Texas city of that size alongside Houston, San Antonio, Dallas and Fort Worth. For latest real estate agents, though, the bigger openings are in suburbs, master-planned developments and up-and-coming markets, not city centers.

Recent findings suggest that no state approved permits for more new homes in 2025 than Texas, which authorized 210,217 units. Dallas and Houston ranked first and second among all U.S. metros, with Austin seventh.

All three metros issued fewer permits than in 2024, yet each is still well ahead of most of the nation. Whole subdivisions are under construction right now, and that work supports agents who sell new builds, partner with builders, focus on master-planned communities, help relocating families or guide people buying their first home.

Statewide active listings were up 2.8% in Q3 2026, and 18 of Texas’ 26 metros saw inventory increase. The median price across the state dipped 0.4% to $333,628, even as 15 metros posted price gains and 12 recorded more sales.

That extra selection lets buyers shop around. Sellers, meanwhile, are counting on their agents to set a smart price, present the home well, get it seen and negotiate effectively.

Among Texas REALTORS® surveyed in 2026, 69% said their buyers faced no competing offers, compared with 57% a year earlier. Seventy-one percent described buyers’ search timelines as ample or reasonable, and only 6% blamed a stalled search on thin inventory.

That changes what clients need from an agent. Outbidding the competition matters less than helping buyers choose well. The agents who stand out have deep neighborhood knowledge, can lay out what different homes will really cost each month and know how to get the most out of builder incentives.

Being a trusted advisor counts for more than processing forms.

International purchasers bought roughly 7,780 Texas homes from April 2025 through March 2026, spending a combined $4 billion. Texas captured 12% of the nation’s international homebuyers over that stretch.

According to recent reports, buyers from Mexico made up the biggest group, with India, China, Nigeria and the U.K. rounding out the top five. More than half, 58%, settled in the suburbs. Agents comfortable with overseas relocations and cross-border transactions have an expanding specialty to tap into, and much of it is in suburban markets.

Texas leaves plenty of room to shape your own business. One agent might become the go-to expert in a single booming suburb. Another might focus on fresh construction where builders are most active, or on families arriving from out of state or relocating within Texas.

Other specialties are open too, from international clients to first-time buyers, move-up buyers and rental investors. You also get to decide whether you’d rather work in a large metro or one of the state’s smaller fast-growing towns.

Whichever direction you choose, expect paychecks to be inconsistent at first. Every specialty depends on regular lead generation and on building relationships over time.

Sources indicate that texas requires aspiring agents to finish 180 hours of qualifying education before they can be licensed. Colibri Real Estate delivers those courses online, so you can fit your studies around the job you already have.

If you choose a package with exam prep, you’ll also get practice exams and live sessions where instructors answer your questions, all aimed at getting you ready to pass.

According to recent reports, building a real estate career in Texas takes effort, and your first years will be spent generating leads and growing your business. Still, if you’re ready to do that work, the conditions are strong: millions of residents relocating, suburbs springing up and homebuilding happening on a massive scale.

It has been revealed that latest households and new housing markets keep appearing across Texas. For agents committed to the work, there’s plenty of room to grow alongside them.

Latest Update: Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.
  • The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine upgrade to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month.
  • Researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:44 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine upgrade to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month. Both versions were pulled from PyPI within about an hour, but anyone who installed them in that window is at risk.

Researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc. have since found that the attacker appears to have gained publishing access using a client certificate and private key for Microsoft’s Engineering System Release Pipeline, an internal service the company uses to sign and publish packages. Address filtering on the service blocked the attacker’s first attempt from Amazon Web Services, according to Wiz, though the attacker was able to publish on a second try from Microsoft-owned address space.

Industry observers note that how the attacker obtained the credentials is not known. Microsoft had not responded to a request for comment from BleepingComputer as of Wednesday.

Industry observers note that the researchers also observed part of the operation, as the attacker’s tooling was reporting its progress to the same public webhook it was using to collect stolen data. The tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source penetration-testing framework that uses AI.

According to recent reports, the malware itself is delivered through a .pth file added to both releases, a type of file Python runs every time it starts, meaning the credential stealer runs even if the framework itself is never imported. The two versions also kept the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0 as a dependency, so the framework continued to work normally while the malware ran in the background.

Industry observers note that once running, the malware collects secrets from environment variables and from other running processes, along with credential files for services such as Azure, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face. It also requests Azure managed identity tokens for 12 resources, according to application security firm Endor Labs Inc., with the second version adding requests for GitHub Actions tokens. The stolen data is then compressed, encoded and sent to a webhook.site address controlled by the attacker.

Researchers at malware tracking site OpenSourceMalware described the malware as a “focused credential and token stealer, not a remote access trojan,” noting that it does not install any persistence on infected systems.

In a recent development, wiz’s analysis suggests the number of victims may be small, though it covers only the 50 requests the attacker’s free webhook.site account retained. Of those, 17 represented only three unique successful thefts of victim data, with the rest coming from the attacker’s own machines and from sandbox and security vendor scanning.

Industry observers note that the incident is not the first this year involving an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Microsoft’s durabletask package was hijacked after its PyPI token was stolen in an attack that has been linked to TeamPCP, the group also behind the compromise of LiteLLM. Wiz notes it has not linked the two incidents.

Anyone who installed either of the malicious versions is being urged to treat it as a credential compromise, according to researchers, who recommend rebuilding from version 1.26.0 and rotating any secrets the affected systems could access.

“A list of dependencies in production might show no trace of the framework, while a build runner could have installed it and been shut down before the alert arrived,” James Matchett, head of security at software supply chain security manufacturer Cloudsmith Ltd., told SiliconANGLE.

“If that runner had access to a deployment token, the team needs to know which version it installed and what the token could access,” he added.

Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.
  • It has been revealed that update, Wednesday Nov.
  • 17: ULA noted Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

It has been revealed that update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA remarked Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA noted Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle firm’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan debuts that Amazon has purchased.

ULA mentioned Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as rapidly as possible.

Amazon Leo stated in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term prepares for Vulcan.”.

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

Industry observers note that ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Sources indicate that spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had introduced 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s Upcoming Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In a recent development, in June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

In a recent development, amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it aims an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security debuts after February.

Recent findings suggest that ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller noted before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under latest leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Industry observers note that amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#6178. Which way is down, revisited

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (746 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Which way is down, revisited

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2008, HousingWire published an analysis asking whether severe mortgage delinquencies were pushing home prices down, or falling prices were pushing delinquencies up.
  • It has been revealed that seventeen of 20 major metros indicated a significant negative correlation between 60-plus-day delinquencies and Case-Shiller prices.
  • According to recent reports, the 2026 market looks very different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2008, HousingWire published an analysis asking whether severe mortgage delinquencies were pushing home prices down, or falling prices were pushing delinquencies up.

It has been revealed that seventeen of 20 major metros indicated a significant negative correlation between 60-plus-day delinquencies and Case-Shiller prices. Granger causality tests found delinquency trends and predicted price trends in 13 metros; six showed a two-way relationship, and only San Francisco showed prices leading delinquencies. In most markets, distress appeared to be part of the mechanism driving prices lower.

According to recent reports, the 2026 market looks very different. Delinquencies are rising year over year while nominal prices still rise nationally. The 2008 relationship may not have vanished, but the housing-credit system may have moved into a different causal regime.

It has been revealed that the Mortgage Bankers Association reported a 4.37% national delinquency rate in the second quarter, 44 basis points above a year earlier. The 90-day rate edged up to 1.43%, foreclosures stood at 0.67% of loans and the seriously delinquent rate rose for a fourth straight quarter.

Yet the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller National Index rose 1.9% year over year in July, the 20-City Composite 2.5% and FHFA’s index 2.6%. Prices have fallen in real terms for 14 straight months, though much of July’s 3.4% inflation was energy-driven; core inflation was 2.5%. The market combines nominal stability, real erosion and rising credit stress, a configuration unlike 2008.

It has been revealed that conventional delinquency was 2.72%, VA 4.89% and FHA 11.79%, with FHA up 122 basis points in a year. ATTOM counted 40,277 foreclosure filings in August, up 13%, with completed foreclosures up 42%. Activity remains far below the 2008–2010 crisis, which helps explain why rising delinquency has not collapsed prices.

Equity is also uneven. ATTOM found 3.2% of mortgaged homes seriously underwater in the second quarter, up from 2.7% a year earlier. Minnesota led at 12.1%, up from 2.6%, while second-ranked Louisiana, at 10.3%, improved from 11.9%. Underwater share measures vulnerability, not distress itself.

Industry observers note that chicago led the Case-Shiller metros in July at 6.9%; Seattle (−1.6), Las Vegas (−1.3) and Denver (−1.1) declined. That 8.5-point spread reflects different regimes within one national economy. A market can carry distress without falling prices if supply is tight, and a falling market can breed delinquency if equity is thin. The relevant unit is the local borrower-market system, not the nation.

In a recent development, the 2008 mechanism was distressed supply: delinquency, foreclosures and REO, lower prices, lower equity, more delinquency. It remains valid, but today’s distressed pipeline is far smaller, so the default-to-price channel may be weaker in aggregate. The reverse channel, in which lower prices erode equity and raise default incentives for leveraged borrowers, may matter more.

The better question is no longer which comes first, but under what conditions the direction changes. One hypothesis: in a normal regime the link is weak; in an equity-stress regime falling prices drive delinquency; in a distressed-supply regime concentrated delinquency drives prices; in a feedback regime both operate at once. That is a framework to test, not a finding.

Whether the 2008 relationship holds today is untested; I am not aware of a published re-estimation across the post-crisis period.

A modern version should use metro-level price and delinquency series from roughly 2000 to 2026, retain the Granger framework for comparability, test for cointegration, add controls for unemployment, mortgage rates, loan type, leverage and equity, and test whether coefficients shift once thresholds such as cumulative price declines, negative equity or serious delinquency are crossed.

This article does not replicate the original tests, which used proprietary loan-level data; comparable public metro delinquency series are not available in the same form.

It has been revealed that in 2008, delinquency, foreclosure and falling prices reinforced one another nationally. In 2026, credit stress is rising while nominal prices hold and metros diverge. The evidence suggests the relationship may have changed; it does not yet show how. Which channel dominates may depend on the state of the market. The question may be less which way is down than when the direction changes, and risk models should treat causality as a function of the regime.

Source: Showalter and Cho, HousingWire, Nov./Dec. 2008. Data as of Oct. 5, 2026.

Young Cho, Ph.D., is the Founder and CEO of PalmBridge Investment.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, spent $228.1 million buying back its STRC preferred stock between Nov. 9 and Nov. 15, according to the tech giant's new filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Over the same period, Strategy bought 485 BTC for $33.4 million, so the company spent almost seven times more on STRC than on Bitcoin.

"Strategy has acquired 485 BTC and repurchased $228M of STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets," Michael Saylor wrote on X.

Industry observers note that the filing highlights that Strategy sold 2.09 million shares of its Class A common stock and raised $244.7 million. The organization used $206.3 million of that amount for STRC buybacks and added another $21.8 million from interest earned on its dollar reserves.

The 485 BTC were bought at an average price of $68,887 per coin. The remaining $5 million from the share sales stayed on the books as free cash.

STRC, also known as Stretch, is a perpetual preferred stock with a variable monthly dividend, and Strategy launched it in July 2025.

It has been revealed that when the price of Bitcoin slipped below $65,000, STRC fell to $99.08. Strategy aims to keep STRC close to its $100 par value, and the company has another $332.2 million set aside for buybacks. The board of Strategy also approved a December STRC dividend at an annual rate of 12%, or $1.00 per share.

"USD Duration is 3.4 yrs and STRC's BTC Credit tightened to 67 bps (-3 bps), assuming 10% BTC ARR, 40% BTC Vol, and a BTC price of $68,800," Saylor added.

As of Nov. 15, Strategy held 850,849 BTC, bought for a total of $64.2 billion at an average price of $75,452 per coin. On Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $63,941, and Strategy's holdings are worth around $54.4 billion.

The unrealized loss of the company on its Bitcoin holdings stands at around $9.8 billion. On Sunday, when the price of Bitcoin fell to $62,029 on Bitfinex, the loss was above $11 billion.

Strategy also holds $4.9 billion in dollar assets, and $4.75 billion of that amount is in its dedicated USD reserve.

Industry News: Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Recent findings suggest that open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Recent findings suggest that open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

In a recent development, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

Sources indicate that for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

Sources indicate that the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

According to recent reports, under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

It has been revealed that the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

Industry observers note that the SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Recent findings suggest that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

Latest Update: Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.
  • In a recent development, it’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows.
  • These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.

In a recent development, it’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”.

Instead, the Copilot as “a newly introduced OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

According to recent reports, the high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the newly introduced Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business blueprint and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” remarked Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

According to recent reports, the end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella mentioned.

In a recent development, the Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authorities in the United States and Canada have revealed a major cross-border crackdown on cryptocurrency fraud, bringing together law enforcement agencies, financial regulators and private companies to target online scam networks.

Sources indicate that the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) declared on Nov. 16 the launch of Operation Niagara, a coordinated initiative aimed at disrupting organized cryptocurrency fraud schemes and protecting potential victims.

According to the Canadian securities regulator, the operation involves investigators, securities specialists and financial crime experts from both countries.

The initiative will use advanced technology and enhanced investigative capabilities to identify fraudulent activity and potential victims in near real time.

Importantly, the operation will not focus solely on investigating criminals after fraud has occurred. Authorities also intend to identify individuals who are being targeted by scammers and intervene before they suffer further financial losses.

"Fraud knows no border, and it targets everyday people," remarked Bonnie Lysyk, Executive Vice-President of Enforcement at the OSC.

The initiative brings together several major law enforcement and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Secret Service, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The newly introduced model, announced Wednesday, reflects the manufacturer’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run.
  • Recent findings suggest that SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:11 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Recent findings suggest that incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc. has announced the launch of SRE-1, a new model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

The newly introduced model, announced Wednesday, reflects the manufacturer’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

Recent findings suggest that SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Industry observers note that resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training, a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan noted Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

Recent findings suggest that in testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

It has been revealed that primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the company. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Up to 80% of paged alerts in production are stated to be handled by Primary On-call without escalation. Customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution, along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%, according to Resolve AI.

In a recent development, salesforce Inc. is among the early customers. Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, remarked that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing, the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team’s paging alerts “without waking an engineer.”.

Recent findings suggest that “No engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production,” stated Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos. “The answer is agents that are accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, and that takes a model built for production.”.

The announcement reflects the Vietnam-based company's commitment to moving beyond software execution toward a more consultative, end-to-end partnership, helping global clients navigate technology complexity, make informed decisions, and implement reliable solutions that deliver lasting business value.

A Changing Role for Technology Partners.

Industry observers note that as AI, cloud technologies, and increasingly interconnected systems reshape business operations, enterprise technology decisions involve greater complexity.
