📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holiday shopping season is in full swing — and it started early this year.

Latest data from specialized point-of-sale software tech giant Quilt Software, which serves more than 20,000 independent retailers, from jewelers and pet stores to liquor stores and grocers, highlighted a 7.6% same-store sales growth spike in October year over year.

That’s in stark contrast to the Q1 through Q3 2.7% to 3.2% bump, which might largely be attributed to inflation, Quilt Software co-founder and CEO Andrew Stern tells Entrepreneur.

What’s more, customers aren’t just getting a head start; they’re also making more frequent shopping trips. Year-over-year transactions per store grew 6% in Q3 and 7.9% in October, per Quilt’s data.

This year, Small Business Saturday, which saw an estimated $18 billion in spending at independent retailers in 2025, falls on November 28, just 27 days before Christmas.

With customers opting for earlier and more frequent purchasing, independent retailers that want to make the most of the limited window need to stay on top of which items are selling in real time to remain ahead of trends and maintain inventory, Stern notes.

The CEO also cautions independent shops against attempting to compete with big-box retailers like Amazon or Walmart on price or convenience, calling it a “race to the bottom.”.

Instead, Stern suggests a two-pronged approach for independent retailers: Lean into what makes them special, and use AI in a way that works for them (it won’t look like it does for mega-retailers).

Recent findings suggest that “ For our small independent merchants, they opened their store for a reason,” Stern says. “They thought they were bringing something really unique that no one else had. So lean into that, because you’re probably right.”.

One in five holiday shoppers strategy to purchase gifts and other holiday items at small or local businesses this year, according to the National Retail Federation’s (NRF) October Holiday Consumer survey.

Shoppers planning to buy from small businesses cited reasons including supporting the community (71%), seeking unique gifts and décor (56%), championing artists through handmade purchases (37%) and finding high-quality products (33%), per the report.

It’s clear that holiday shoppers want what independent retailers have to offer — but it’s crucial that those stores put themselves on people’s radar.

It has been revealed that “ Make sure that [customers] can see you, that you’re visible when people do their Google searches, or increasingly their ChatGPT searches,” Stern says. “Make sure that you come up because they want to find you.”.

In a recent development, nowadays, independent retailers must have an answer engine optimization (AEO) strategy to stay relevant and show up in search results. Earlier this month, Entrepreneur spoke with Courtney Sandora, founder of digital marketing agency Go Social, to learn more about how brands can compete in the AEO landscape.

Sandora notes that customers use LLM-powered search engines to ask specific questions, so savvy businesses should hone in on the queries they can reliably and successfully own, “seeding” stories and copy that bolster their authority.

According to recent reports, “That storytelling extends across everything from PR to creators, even how you appear on a retailer website,” Sandora states. “Typically, on retailer websites, there’s a short description. Is the message you want to tell in that retailer website description? Consistency matters.”.

It’s critical that small businesses use rapidly advancing AI technologies to their advantage.

However, that won’t look exactly like it does for major retailers, which might harness AI to manage six-month supply chains or optimize warehouse logistics, Stern says.

Instead, independent retailers should focus on taking small steps with significant impact, like using agentic solutions to outsource specific tasks they might not have time to execute to their fullest potential.

For example, the right AI tool can give shop owners the marketing support they’ve never had, unfolding in the background as they help customers at the counter. Quilt offers its retailers an AI marketing assistant that can create campaigns for customers with their own inventory.

Industry observers note that “ This generative AI is able to create copy that’s in their voice,” Stern says, “that’s tailored to different cohorts of customers and can say, ‘Hey, come in, I think we have some products that you might be interested in. Here they are.’”.

Quilt also offers an AI assistant that can help small retailers navigate unwieldy piles of inventory.

Recent findings suggest that stern points to thrift stores, which tend to rely on volunteer staff to sift through large amounts of donations quickly, as an example. Shops can snap a picture of a leather couch and receive a price estimate immediately.

The AI tool can also help them identify rare and valuable items that might otherwise go unnoticed. “ We’ve had some crazy cases like, ‘Oh, that looks like a Tiffany lamp. Look at the bottom of it and see if there’s a signature that says Tiffany. If so, do not charge $5 for that lamp,’” Stern says.

The NRF expects retail sales in November and December to grow 4.2% over 2025, for a total spending surpassing $1 trillion. That’s a massive opportunity for independent retailers that opt out of competition with big-box retailers and leverage the data to win their share.

The holiday shopping season is in full swing — and it started early this year.

New data from specialized point-of-sale software manufacturer Quilt Software, which serves more than 20,000 independent retailers, from jewelers and pet stores to liquor stores and grocers, showed a 7.6% same-store sales growth spike in October year over year.

That’s in stark contrast to the Q1 through Q3 2.7% to 3.2% bump, which might largely be attributed to inflation, Quilt Software co-founder and CEO Andrew Stern tells Entrepreneur.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, head west out of Paris, and well-heeled suburbs give way to sleepy commuter towns.
  • In a recent development, turn north from there and you arrive at the small town of Cergy, where MBS inked a €6 billion deal in August to build three theme parks, apartment blocks, hotels, and infrastructure upgrades.
  • The town is not alone in tapping funds thousands of miles away—for good reason: For the past decade, the pool of Saudi money has seemed bottomless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, head west out of Paris, and well-heeled suburbs give way to sleepy commuter towns. There, two dots on the map illustrate one of the most dizzying pipelines of wealth on the planet: Saudi Arabia. About 14 miles outside the capital sits Château Louis XIV, a close copy of the nearby real thing in Versailles; Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bought the Château in 2015 for $300 million.

In a recent development, turn north from there and you arrive at the small town of Cergy, where MBS inked a €6 billion deal in August to build three theme parks, apartment blocks, hotels, and infrastructure upgrades. “This project is designed to breathe new life into the territory,” Jean-Paul Jeandon, the area’s president, told me one rainy October evening. Without the Saudi deal, he said, Cergy faced poor growth prospects.

The town is not alone in tapping funds thousands of miles away—for good reason: For the past decade, the pool of Saudi money has seemed bottomless. With a steady influx of cash from vast oil reserves, the kingdom’s Public Investment Fund, or PIF—of which MBS is chairman—has seen its assets rocket 600% since 2015, to more than $900 billion, and has splurged on soccer, tech giants, California EV manufacturer Lucid, London’s Heathrow Airport, and numerous other investments, all while building mega-size tourism sites, arenas, and entertainment complexes back home.

It has been revealed that driving the action has been one defining project: Vision 2030, MBS’s signature strategy to transform the country by ending its overwhelming dependence on oil. No investment has seemed too major or costly; in fact, mammoth spending was the point: It positioned Saudi Arabia as a major player in tech, AI, entertainment, and other fields. Host the six-month World Expo extravaganza in 2030 in Riyadh? And the 2034 FIFA World Cup? The answer to both: We must.

According to recent reports, but that giant pool may be drying up, and with it, Saudi Arabia’s splashiest plans for remaking its economy. After a decade of frenzied spending, MBS’s ambitions have been battered by the Iran war and Houthi attacks, rattling the kingdom’s business partners and other foreigners, including the millions of visitors the country had touted as proof of its transformation. Increasingly, Saudi officials worry whether businesses will seek partners elsewhere, rather than risk being embroiled in a country at war. If they do, the impact will be felt long after peace returns, not only by 36 million Saudis, but global business too, especially in the U.S., the biggest recipient of Saudi investment.

According to recent reports, companies will need to hunt hard for funding as deep as the PIF’s. The UAE’s sovereign wealth fund, an obvious alternative, is also feeling the war’s strain. “There is no obvious, equally large capital source waiting in the wings,” the Council on Foreign Relations warned in May.

According to recent reports, the success of Vision 2030 rests on breaking the country’s isolation and cementing its global clout. When MBS unveiled the plan in 2015, the logic was clear: With 71% of Saudis younger than 35, millions more jobs were needed, including for women (who were finally allowed to drive). Entire new sectors—tourism, entertainment, sports—were necessary to break the dependence on oil and to stop fun-starved Saudis from blowing an estimated $1 billion a year traveling abroad to go to the movies and sample good restaurants.

Sources indicate that A decade into MBS’s rule, the country remains an autocracy that sentences even mild critics to long prison terms and regularly executes nonviolent offenders. So even if MBS’s Vision 2030 dreams falter, his own grip is firm.

Despite that, witnessing the kingdom’s transformation up close has been a startling experience.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, a business consultant I met in a hotel lobby gawked at a speaker that was piping in soft music—until then forbidden under Saudi Islamic rules. By 2021, thousands were attending live concerts and dozens of AMC multiplexes had cropped up, ending a 35-year ban on cinemas. At the inaugural Formula 1 race in Jeddah in 2021, I gaped at dancers in skintight, hot-pink bodysuits gyrating on stage to ear-blasting DJ sets. And in 2024, when I asked Munira Aldayood, Riyadh’s director of conferences and exhibitions, why she’d returned home after 23 years of living in the U.S., her answer probably would have stunned people a decade earlier. “As a female, Saudi Arabia is now the best place to live,” she noted. “It’s heaven.”.

But for all Vision 2030’s ambitions, the country is still heavily dependent on oil. Oil production, fully controlled by the state-owned Saudi Aramco—whose strategy is overseen by MBS—still constitutes 60% of fiscal revenue, billions of which have been transferred to the PIF to pay for Vision 2030 projects. “Oil is the enabler of everything,” indicates Helima Croft, RBC Capital Markets’ global head of commodity strategy.

It has been revealed that but oil is also a wartime vulnerability. The sharp rise in oil prices pushed Aramco’s third-quarter profits up 9%. Yet the war’s deleterious effects inside Saudi Arabia became clear not long after the U.S. and Israel dropped bombs on Iran last February. Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz to critical oil shipments, forcing Saudi Arabia to cut millions of barrels in exports a day or to pipe them overland to its Red Sea port. Glittering Vision 2030 events, geared to attracting global talent and tourists, were shelved. The PIF dropped its $5 billion LIV Golf investment in May, ditching efforts to acquire the PGA and sign top players. It rescheduled an international tennis tournament, postponed a film festival in Jeddah, and canceled the city’s Formula 1 race. Foreign direct investment into Saudi Arabia plunged 18% in the second quarter, and the country predicts its economy will shrink 3.6% this year, its steepest drop since the pandemic, with a $51 billion budget shortfall. “A lot of investment will sit on the sidelines and wait for some more signs of stability,” says Monica Malik, chief economist at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank.

According to recent reports, riyadh, meanwhile, was closing its own wallet. The PIF set out to limit foreign investments to 20%, down from 30% in 2020; it withdrew its planned $200 million partnership with Upcoming York City’s Metropolitan Opera.

But for a time, the belt-tightening seemed isolated. The PIF kept spending, especially in the U.S. It plowed $10 billion into the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in April, snapped up $26.3 million worth of SpaceX shares in June, and in August completed its $55 billion takeover of Electronic Arts, the Silicon Valley gaming giant.

That all suggested the Saudi bonanza would continue regardless. For companies looking for funding, “they believed it was an easy ATM,” says Croft.

It has been revealed that the flaws in that belief became stunningly clear one steamy afternoon in October, when Houthi rebels in Yemen fired a ballistic missile into Riyadh’s international airport—a core project of Vision 2030—killing 12 people outright. A second missile hit the airport the next day, forcing a shutdown and stranding thousands. Days later, a missile hit Saudi Aramco’s headquarters, forcing the world’s biggest oil organization to evacuate its sprawling campus.

Sources indicate that by late October, the PIF had canceled the country’s flagship business conference, the Future Investment Initiative, or FII, after it emerged that few Wall Street hedge funders or corporate execs dared risk traveling to the so-called Davos in the Desert. Aramco’s office in Riyadh was hit on Nov. 8. Reeling from the strikes, the PIF scrapped five of the multibillion-dollar stadiums it had promised to build for the 2034 World Cup. Even if peace returns, “they are going to be very focused on their own citizens, their own infrastructure needs,” says Croft.

According to recent reports, for investors who’ve long become accustomed to bloated sovereign wealth funds in the Gulf, it will be a tough adjustment. In the PIF, U.S. execs found a ready taker for their startups and expansions. Buying into SpaceX’s public listing tripled the PIF’s U.S. holdings to $38.9 billion.

In fact, the Saudis have plowed billions into Silicon Valley startups in the past decade. The PIF’s $3.5 billion investment in Uber in 2016 helped power the manufacturer’s global growth, giving the fund a seat on the board and cementing close ties with Big Tech.

But the Iran war could change all that. With bombs hitting Saudi oil pipelines and refineries, “there’s going to be less to go around in terms of sovereign wealth funds cutting big checks for asset managers and hedge funds overseas,” Croft states.

In a recent development, trying to calm jittery markets in October, Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman (MBS’s half-brother) told industry representatives: “The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist.” But foreign businesses are far less blasé after the airport attacks. “If you’re a potential investor looking at a Vision 2030 project, and you see the main gateway attacked, you’ll say, ‘Well, I’ll invest in Singapore or Sweden,’” says James Reeve, a senior PIF director in Riyadh until last January.

It has been revealed that flying over Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield in 2017, I was stunned by its vastness, with rigs and pipelines stretching to the Persian Gulf. “We are cut off from the world,” Shaybah manager Khalid Al-Jamea told me. But the war has shown that sense of isolation was illusory. In October, Houthi rebels aimed a drone at Shaybah from 600 miles away, killing two oil workers before Saudi air-defense weapons shot it down.

No such dangers exist in Cergy, outside Paris. There, locals gathered one rainy October evening to debate whether to back the PIF’s projects, voicing concerns about traffic, pollution, and inflated rents. For the kingdom, the worries are more existential—including whether MBS’s grand strategy for his country can stay on track.

Industry News: Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am.

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey remarked he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Recent findings suggest that humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey mentioned today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”.

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The tech giant says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”.

In a recent development, greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

It has been revealed that humphrey remarked the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian revealed a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey stated. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”.

Sources indicate that he acknowledged that following through on the initiative for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the manufacturer’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”.

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey remarked that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he noted. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.
  • At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot highlights its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT.
  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot highlights its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

Sources indicate that if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

Industry observers note that it highlights how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own consumers. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

According to recent reports, while the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:.

Sources indicate that the first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Recent findings suggest that why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

Sources indicate that the striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, revealed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance indicates it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

Sources indicate that what the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It highlights the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance states the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest enhancement says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

Recent findings suggest that the design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Industry observers note that binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

Industrial monitoring startup BrightAI closes $97M investment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.
  • Industry observers note that smith Point Capital led the Series A round.
  • Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:37 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Industry observers note that smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, problems often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

According to recent reports, the first component of the firm’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for problems that can’t be detected visually.

The motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and  vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the tech giant, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

According to recent reports, brightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for  example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The tech giant’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer notes that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

Recent findings suggest that the third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

In a recent development, “Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” mentioned founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”.

BrightAI says that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, looks to expand its use of the organization’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

Industry observers note that nvidia could be about to hand its biggest job to the man who helped turn Arm into one of the world’s most valuable chip companies. Rene Haas is now being considered as a potential successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia, a familiar face at the center of the AI industry’s biggest leadership change.

Industry observers note that bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s recruitment firm had approached Haas as part of its search for a new chief executive. Haas previously spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since overseen its expansion into the booming AI infrastructure market.

Rene Haas has been approached regarding the CEO role at Nvidia by recruiting firm Heidrick & Struggles, which was hired by the board to replace Jensen Huang https://t.co/yiJ6NkvEtS.

An appointment would put someone with experience at both companies in charge of Nvidia’s next chapter. But what does it mean for crypto? Could Haas push the AI boom even further, and what would that mean for Bitcoin and the rest of the market?

Haas is not an outsider to Nvidia. He previously ran the company’s computing products business between 2006 and 2013, giving him direct experience with the company before its transformation into an AI powerhouse.

In a recent development, his subsequent run at Arm offers a glimpse of what he might bring to the role. Arm reported $4.92 billion in revenue for its fiscal 2026, up from $4.01 billion the previous year. Its profit before tax climbed from $756 million to $960 million. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am.
  • Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup released by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel intends — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.
  • Industry observers note that that includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am.

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup released by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel intends — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

Industry observers note that that includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The manufacturer notes Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, remarked last month that it looks to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

According to recent reports, companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

Industry observers note that when Vayo released last month, Fridgen stated it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo notes no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister tech giant Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

Recent findings suggest that for flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the manufacturer says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company states. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

In a recent development, payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever organization they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

The service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

It has been revealed that his co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it released last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the tech giant notes it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After an crucial hackathon that demonstrated how AI agents could autonomously perform payments using blockchain, global payments giant Mastercard has spotlighted the XRP Ledger (XRPL).
  • At the XRP Ledger Hackathon, developers used Mastercard Agent Pay for machines to explore newly introduced possibilities for micropayments and autonomous commerce, including how AI agents can transact within defined spending limits and with verified merchants.
  • Global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After an crucial hackathon that demonstrated how AI agents could autonomously perform payments using blockchain, global payments giant Mastercard has spotlighted the XRP Ledger (XRPL).

36 hours. 179 hackers. 70 submissions. At the XRP Ledger Hackathon, developers used Mastercard Agent Pay for machines to explore newly introduced possibilities for micropayments and autonomous commerce, including how AI agents can transact within defined spending limits and with verified merchants. See what we learned about the future of agentic commerce: https://t.co/S4NwQxxuRi #AgenticCommerce #DigitalAssets #AI.

Global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon. In the post, the payments firm detailed that 179 developers submitted 70 projects during the 36-hour event in Manhattan.

The focus of the competition was how to enable AI-powered agents to autonomously execute transactions and micropayments, engage with verified merchants and so forth, all while operating within budgets set by developers.

The hackathon was held as part of the preparations for Ripple’s annual conference called Swell. Mastercard, Amazon Web Services, QuickNode and Ledger supported the event, which had a prize pool of over $40,000.

Mastercard published an official article in which it mentioned the challenge given to developers. They had to build AI agents that could autonomously make payments to verified merchants without human input.

Also, the agents had to operate within a specified budget. They had to settle payments using Ripple’s USD-backed stablecoin called RLUSD. They had to do this on the XRP Ledger.

In a recent development, one of the purposes of the challenge was to showcase how blockchain infrastructure can enable micropayments. This is especially the case for micropayments smaller than one cent.

In the future, these micropayments could be valuable as AI agents start buying computational resources or requesting data from other AI agents and then making payments themselves for digital services.

Mastercard’s vice president of digital assets, Michael Broderick, stressed that the company's technology called Agent Pay for Machines could enable such payments.

In a recent development, the project that won the competition is called Wraps. Its creators are Adarsha Mishra and Hrishabh Ayush. Their project dealt with how to secure user privacy in AI-based transactions. Their project demonstrated a method to prove that search logs were not being saved.

One of the most interesting things mentioned in the Mastercard report might be how the XRP Ledger is increasingly being used for payments by machines.

Mastercard mentioned that over 500,000 transactions are being conducted daily on the XRPL by AI agents.

Also, it’s reported that Ripple has recorded over 10 million payments using the x402 internet payment protocol on XRPL. This comes less than three months after the protocol crossed the 1 million payment milestone on the network.

#6133. M&A Isn’t Just for Substantial Companies. Here’s How Startups Can Do It With No Cash.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

M&A Isn’t Just for Substantial Companies. Here’s How Startups Can Do It With No Cash.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Recent findings suggest that most startups are so focused on building stand-alone businesses through traditional sales and marketing that they overlook other ways to grow, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&A).
  • This article will provide a high-level tutorial on what M&A is, why you should consider it, and how to negotiate deals that can get to the finish line, even if you are not large enough to be bankable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that most startups are so focused on building stand-alone businesses through traditional sales and marketing that they overlook other ways to grow, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&A). They simply have not been trained on the topic and don’t know that, for some businesses, it can be a faster, more effective way to scale.

This article will provide a high-level tutorial on what M&A is, why you should consider it, and how to negotiate deals that can get to the finish line, even if you are not large enough to be bankable.

Recent findings suggest that A merger is a combination of the shareholders of two businesses into one. A merger typically involves combining the management teams and operations into one. An acquisition is exactly what it sounds like: your business is acquiring a company (or being acquired by one), with the acquiring team retaining 100% control over all key decisions in the latest company. The acquired company’s operations will be integrated into the new company, however the acquiring company sees fit, as the buying company will control all decisions post-transaction. So, you will need to decide which scenario will work best for your needs.

M&A has many advantages, the key ones being speed, economies of scale and removing competition. Since the acquired business is already up and running and, hopefully, producing cash flow, it offers a much faster path to growth. For example, if a restaurant chain was trying to grow from 1 to 2 locations, it would take them over a year to find a site and build it out. But through M&A, that second location is already built and is immediately generating revenues today.

Furthermore, when you combine two businesses, you can eliminate duplicative costs and achieve economies of scale. For example, you don’t need two executive teams, two insurance policies, two marketing agencies, two accounting firms, etc. By removing these duplicative costs, the combined business will end up with a more profitable bottom-line margin, where hopefully 1+1=3.

As for the competitive advantages, by buying a competitor in the market, that will increase your market share and have you competing against one less competitor (which may help your pricing). As an example, in my hometown of Cary, NC, one entrepreneur acquired and rolled up around 20 competing Mexican restaurants, with the goal of ensuring that no matter which Mexican restaurant you ate at, he was getting the sale, with nearly 100% market share.

That all mentioned, things can go wrong with M&A. Be sure to read my prior article on the potential pitfalls with M&A, so you don’t get into any trouble here, and you go into this M&A direction “eyes wide open” to prepare for potential hurdles that may arise in the future.

Depending on the size of the transaction, M&A can be funded either from the buyer’s cash account, or by raising additional capital from investors, or with no cash at all via an exchange of equity between the two businesses. Since most start-ups don’t generate much profit, it is unlikely they will be bankable. So, this last path of exchanging equity makes it possible for companies of any size to pursue M&A without any financing required at all.

The key thing about M&A is that it does not necessarily need to be dependent on economic or financial market conditions. Even if third-party investors have paused upcoming investments during a down market, nothing prevents two businesses from merging in a cashless transaction at any time. So, if you can’t raise capital for your stand-alone restaurant chain growth, you can still be growing using M&A as the driver of that growth.

Recent findings suggest that for established businesses generating revenue and profits, it is pretty easy to value those companies using historical revenue or profit multiples from past transactions in your industry. For example, if most small restaurants are sold at 3x EBITDA, it is reasonable to assume your small restaurant can be valued at 3x EBITDA. A good business broker can advise you on what the normal multipliers will be for the size of your company’s revenues, profits, and growth rate.

According to recent reports, if you don’t have revenues or profits to value, then you need to use another metric. Maybe that is cash invested in the business, or asset value, or the assets themselves. For example, if one real estate owner has 4 locations and another real estate owner has 2 locations, then perhaps those two businesses could be combined into one business where the 4-location business owned 67% and the 2-location business owned 33% of the newly introduced company.

It has been revealed that let’s say two self-storage businesses are exploring a merger. One does $6MM in revenue, $1MM in profit, and has 300,000 square feet of buildings (all mature, open for many years). The other has $2MM in revenue, $0 in profit today (but will end up at $1MM after they fully rent out their space) and also has 300,000 square feet of buildings (but they are brand newly introduced still ramping up clients and revenues).

According to recent reports, how do you value this? On revenues, it would be 80/20. On profits, it would be 100/0, and on square footage it would be 50/50. If I were the buyer, I would start the ownership at 75/25, and if the smaller business successfully increases its client base per its plan, it can earn its way up to 50/50 through an earn-out. That seems to be the fairest for all parties; that should get both parties to the finish line.

I am a former investment banker on Wall Street, and M&A is incorporated into my DNA. It is something I am comfortable with, as I have bought and sold many companies over my entrepreneurial career. But if you are a first-timer here, I know it can be “scary.”  But it doesn’t need to be. Surround yourself with smart M&A advisors who have “been there and done that,” both in terms of negotiating M&A and integrating companies post M&A, and everything should turn out just fine.

Recent findings suggest that and hopefully your shareholders will thank you for materially accelerating your growth and helping them to expand their valuation multipliers as a bigger company. Good luck!

#6132. Warby Parker is betting its next chapter on smart glasses people actually want to wear

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (811 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Warby Parker is betting its next chapter on smart glasses people actually want to wear

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warby Parker is one of the clear winners of the 2010s-era direct-to-consumer (DTC) wave.
  • While many of its peers from that era have struggled or shut down, Warby Parker retains an empire of 360 stores; its revenue increased 10% to $245 million in its most recent quarter.
  • In a recent development, in search of its next substantial growth engine, Warby Parker is planting its flag in the promising but still tiny market for smart glasses, teaming up with Google.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warby Parker is one of the clear winners of the 2010s-era direct-to-consumer (DTC) wave. It and other upstart digital-first brands like Allbirds shoes, Away luggage, and Casper mattresses used e-commerce savvy to cut out middlemen like wholesalers, upending their industries and selling straight to shoppers.

While many of its peers from that era have struggled or shut down, Warby Parker retains an empire of 360 stores; its revenue increased 10% to $245 million in its most recent quarter. Still, the eyewear company is grappling with soft growth in fresh active customers—only 3.4% last quarter—and a sluggish eyewear market overall.

In a recent development, in search of its next substantial growth engine, Warby Parker is planting its flag in the promising but still tiny market for smart glasses, teaming up with Google. The tech behemoth, along with partner Samsung, will provide the AI technology behind the glasses, including a high-resolution display tucked inside one lens that wearers can control with a wristband or watch.

For Warby Parker, whose own innovations have included a virtual try-on and features that enable customers to choose glasses from home, the partnership could bolster its tech-forward reputation, tapping its strengths in design and retail to win eyeglass buyers of the future.

Recent findings suggest that “Glasses are the original wearable, right?” says Warby Parker co-founder and co-CEO Neil Blumenthal on Fortune’s Behind the Business YouTube series. “The combination of form and function is something we can bring to this new category and create something that has a ton of technology in it.”.

It has been revealed that the Warby Parker glasses, which will start at $395, hit the market on Nov. 12 and are taking on an early market leader in Meta, whose Ray-Ban smart glasses are designed and made in partnership with Italy’s EssilorLuxottica, the largest eyewear tech giant in the world. Meta’s glasses represented about 69% of smart glasses so far this year. EssilorLuxottica has noted it sold 7 million pairs of AI-supported glasses last year.

Google’s and Meta’s decisions to team up with established eyewear brands like Warby Parker and EssilorLuxottica demonstrate that they understand that so-called intelligent eyewear, as Warby Parker refers to it, must be aesthetically pleasing and less sci-fi-like to achieve mass appeal.

“We’ve always innovated in technology,” says Dave Gilboa, Warby Parker’s other co-CEO and co-founder. “But our north star is that someone has to want to put this on their face.”.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, the “smart” aspect of the Warby Parker glasses is subtle. The cameras on the front of the frame could pass for a screw. Wearers can start filming or take a photograph with the glasses by pressing a small button near the temple. Outward-facing lights illuminate when the user is recording, a feature that helps assuage concerns that wearers will use smart glasses to photograph or film surreptitiously.

Recent findings suggest that warby Parker commands just 1% of the U.S. eyewear market, but its history as a digital-first brand and its reputation for simple but nice-looking design have made it a desirable partner for Significant Tech, states Kate Winick, an analyst with Forrester Research.

It has been revealed that “Warby Parker is a small player, but it’s the right player,” says Winick. “It has stores in these zip codes that tech companies desperately want to reach.’.

In a recent development, that’s especially vital for Google, which has a lot riding on these glasses. The company needs Warby Parker, Winick indicates, to help it move past Google Glass, its first attempt at smart glasses, which flopped after its 2013 debut. Glass was bulky, its battery died quickly, and at $1,500 it was hard to justify. Worse, it made people uneasy: many bars, restaurants, and theaters banned it over fears of non-consensual recording. It came to embody the era’s “tech bro” stereotype so completely that its wearers earned a nickname: “glassholes.”.

Google is eager for its new version of smart glasses to prove that its technology can work at scale across other wearables. Forrester’s Winick expects tech giants to use the wearable tech featured in glasses in other devices, such as Meta’s Muse Charm, a pocket- and keychain-sized AI companion.

Recent findings suggest that at Warby Parker’s recent quarterly check-in with Wall Street analysts, where smart glasses dominated the discussion, the tech giant said smart glasses could contribute several percentage points to its fourth-quarter growth. (Google and Warby Parker have not disclosed the revenue sharing and intellectual property ownership details of their partnership.).

In a recent development, blumenthal and Gilboa acknowledge the privacy concerns smart glasses raise, but they argue the devices could also fix a modern habit: constantly reaching for our phones. “For the first time, you can have this accessory that enables you to leave your phone in your pocket to keep your attention in the real world,” Gilboa states.

CFTC Makes Historic Move With Blockchain Derivatives Approval

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (366 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.
  • According to recent reports, on Nov.
  • According to recent reports, as per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 16, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig unveiled that the commission had given the green light to exchange (designated contract market or DCM) and clearinghouse (derivatives clearing organization or DCO) applications for a company using blockchain technology for the execution and settlement of derivatives contracts.

According to recent reports, as per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S. financial markets. He said that blockchain-based market infrastructure is compatible with current U.S. financial regulations.

"This approval makes clear that there is a regulatory path for companies that want to innovate and use blockchain technology to modernize how derivatives are traded and settled,"  he elaborated.

According to recent reports, selig pointed out that the U.S. derivatives markets have seen a number of technological advancements, from physical trading floors to electronic trading platforms.

Now, with blockchain technology, he believes there is an opportunity to further modernize financial market infrastructure without losing regulatory oversight and investor protections.

Notably, there is no technical architecture requirement imposed on derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses under the CFTC's current regulatory framework.

Therefore, firms that leverage blockchain-based networks can apply for regulatory approval under the same set of rules and regulations that apply to traditional financial market participants.

However, Selig also clarified that blockchain adoption is not a license to escape regulatory oversight.

Companies will still need to comply with rules covering anti-money laundering (AML), client protections, market monitoring, risk mitigation and other measures designed to protect the integrity of financial markets.

Simply put, the CFTC is looking to bring blockchain technology into regulated derivatives market infrastructure while maintaining the same standards as traditional financial market participants.

For some time, the CFTC chairman has been pushing for a scenario where U.S. companies developing emerging financial technologies can operate in the country without having to look to international markets.

The latest developments further reinforce the message that the U.S. is open for business for companies building blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, according to Selig.

Seattle fleet tracking tech giant Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who notes HQ is staying put

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.
  • Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a newly introduced CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.
  • Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no intends to change that.” He said he visits the firm’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a newly introduced CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no intends to change that.” He said he visits the firm’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Recent findings suggest that consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based company acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Recent findings suggest that consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software firm Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and notes it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli mentioned Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Industry observers note that zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the firm.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but stated Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Recent findings suggest that zonar has added 1,000 latest customers so far this year, a spokesperson stated. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 blueprint, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli mentioned.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli remarked Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He noted those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the significant players.”.

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

Industry observers note that “Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”.

Sources indicate that founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The manufacturer cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • According to recent reports, most stablecoin debuts promise a token that never moves.
  • It has been revealed that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

According to recent reports, most stablecoin debuts promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

It has been revealed that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The manufacturer claims R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery mentioned the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

In a recent development, the model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the firm, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

According to recent reports, ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as newly introduced rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he stated, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

According to recent reports, "Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

It has been revealed that the OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

Industry observers note that eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

In a recent development, eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent firm, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU rolled out earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

It has been revealed that the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

Recent findings suggest that the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

In a recent development, eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

#6127. Breaking: I’ve Been a CFO, a CPA, a Franchisee and a CEO — Here Are the Credentials That Get You Hired Now

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1173 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: I’ve Been a CFO, a CPA, a Franchisee and a CEO — Here Are the Credentials That Get You Hired Now

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • I’ve had a lot of impressive titles.
  • Sources indicate that early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve had a lot of impressive titles. But titles describe what you’ve already done. In today’s AI-driven market, decision-makers want proof of how you think, who will vouch for you and what you’ll do next.

Sources indicate that early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking. I became a CPA with a global Massive 6 firm and then worked my way into CFO and CEO roles. Later, I became a franchise business owner and learned more about grit, determination and humility than I had in the previous 20 years combined.

Each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.

In a recent development, I see this play out every week. As a franchise consultant, I spend most of my time with directors, vice presidents and CXOs, many of them facing a restructuring. Their resumes are stacked. Yet the ones who land on their feet fastest, whether that means a upcoming role, a board seat or a franchise award, rarely win on titles. They win on a different set of credentials, and some of those can be built in months, not decades.

Here are the four I’ve seen matter most.

A title says you held a job. A point of view shows how you thought while you held it. When I was a CFO at a real estate developer, my work was buried in spreadsheets and board meetings. Nobody outside the building knew how I approached the cash crunch during the Great Recession or difficult acquisitions.

Sources indicate that when I started my national consulting firm, I had no choice but to put my thinking in public. I began posting regularly on LinkedIn about franchise ownership, career transitions and the lessons learned as a franchisee. That consistency, more than any credential on my profile, is why strangers started calling. More than 20,000 people now follow me, and many executives tell me they read my posts long before reaching out to me.

Industry observers note that pick two or three topics where your experience gives you a unique viewpoint and write about them every week. You aren’t building an audience for its own sake. You’re creating a searchable record of your expertise.

Earlier in my career, my network was mostly people I’d worked with directly. That works until you’re in transition or need help outside your industry, which is exactly when most people need it. I learned this through three reorganizations. Three of the four companies I worked for over 26 years no longer exist. So I started nurturing my network long before I needed it.

Industry observers note that franchisors taught me this lesson from the other side of the table. When candidates apply to buy a franchise, the franchisor evaluates them just as carefully as the candidate evaluates the brand. The candidates who move through smoothly are the ones other people will vouch for — former colleagues, bankers and existing owners in the system.

This is where LinkedIn Premium has earned a spot in my toolkit. I use Sales Navigator to find and follow the executives I serve and to identify mutual connections who could make a warm introduction. I don’t use it to blast messages. I use it to find a valued connection who can vouch for me, and then I ask that person directly.

Sources indicate that think of 25 people who will take your call tomorrow. If fewer than half of them work outside your current organization, start widening the circle now, while you don’t need favors. And never send a message that doesn’t offer the other person something of value.

It has been revealed that this credential surprises executives the most. As a CEO, I had people build the model, chase the receivables and fix the website. As a fitness franchise owner, I was the OEO — the Only Executive Officer — and I tell my candidates to expect the same.

Hiring managers and franchisors are asking a version of the same question: Will this person roll up their sleeves and do the work, not just direct it? You answer that with evidence. Maybe you’ve run a side project, advised a small business or built your own department or systems.

Recent findings suggest that today I run a national practice largely on my own. The tools I pay for earn their keep only because they let one person do the work a small team used to do.

Identify one hands-on accomplishment from the past two years that didn’t depend on a team and make it visible.

In a recent development, the fastest way to look obsolete is to describe how things were done a decade ago. The old adage “if it isn’t broken, don’t fix it” doesn’t apply today. The executives I see winning today are adaptable. One of my candidates just bought a second franchise in a different industry because she has an insatiable appetite for learning.

Sources indicate that after more than 30 years in business, I’m still learning. I’m working on a second edition of my book because some of my original advice needs updating. Admitting that isn’t a weakness. It tells people I’m paying attention.

Industry observers note that be ready to explain, in two sentences, something you’ve learned in the past six months and how you’ve applied it. I’m not dismissing traditional credentials. My CPA background is the reason candidates trust me to walk them through financing options. My years as a CFO and CEO gave me pattern recognition no course could teach.

But titles are only a starting point. They tell people what you’ve done. The four points above tell them what you’ll do next.

Sources indicate that start this week. Write one post that shares a real lesson from your career. Reach out to three people outside your company. Add something to your profile that you built, not just something you managed. Those small moves compound faster than you’d expect.

Sources indicate that if you want a head start, LinkedIn’s Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to find the ones that fit the way you work.

It has been revealed that I’ve had a lot of impressive titles. But titles describe what you’ve already done. In today’s AI-driven market, decision-makers want proof of how you think, who will vouch for you and what you’ll do next.

Early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking. I became a CPA with a global Big 6 firm and then worked my way into CFO and CEO roles. Later, I became a franchise business owner and learned more about grit, determination and humility than I had in the previous 20 years combined.

Recent findings suggest that each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.
