Industry News: One in four boomers are still working well into their 70s because they can’t afford to retire—around 10% have even picked up second jobs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, turning 60 meant one thing: finally winding down and enjoying the fruits of your labor.
  • Sources indicate that in fact, more than one in four (27%) Americans aged 60 to 75 say they can’t afford to retire, according to a upcoming snap poll by Resume Builder.
  • Unsurprisingly, it’s not because they miss the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, turning 60 meant one thing: finally winding down and enjoying the fruits of your labor. But now a significant chunk of would-be retirees are working well into their 70s because they can’t afford to kick up their feet in the current economy.

Sources indicate that in fact, more than one in four (27%) Americans aged 60 to 75 say they can’t afford to retire, according to a upcoming snap poll by Resume Builder. Instead of going part-time and easing up, nearly 10% have found second jobs or additional income streams. And 12% who have already retired are now considering returning to work.

Unsurprisingly, it’s not because they miss the office.

Among those still working, looking for work, or considering a return, 28% cite the high cost of living as their main reason—and it’s not because they were all financially reckless.

According to recent reports, worryingly, nearly 20% of respondents admitted they have no retirement savings at all. But they’re in the minority.

More than half of the respondents haven’t dipped into their retirement savings early, and just 15% say they haven’t saved enough for retirement.

But prices keep climbing, and the nest egg they have now may not stretch to cover years —or rather, decades — of not working, especially if they want a retirement with holidays and the odd luxury, not just pottering around the house on the bare minimum.

Despite working for decades, 37% say they don’t have enough money to maintain an “acceptable standard of living” if they quit and retire right now.

It’s not just the current high cost of living keeping people in jobs longer than they’d like. It’s the fear of what’s coming next: 17% worry Social Security will change, and 16% fear healthcare costs will rise.

And actually, some 18% of the boomers surveyed are working simply because they want to—be it for organization, purpose or extra pocket money.

In the U.S., the number of people still working past 65 has quadrupled since the 1980s, according to Pew Research Center. Almost 20% of Americans 65 and older are now employed, nearly double the share who were working 35 years ago.

Industry observers note that but the trend stretches across the Atlantic. In the U.K., nearly 20% of baby boomers and late Gen Xers are similarly “unretiring”—or planning to, because their retirement desires don’t match up to the nest egg they’ve built.

It’s why it’s never too soon to start retirement planning.

Renowned financial expert Suze Orman previously highlighted that Gen Z and millennials could retire as millionaires if they make the most of compound growth while they’re young.

She used just $100 to highlight how powerful compound growth is.

Sources indicate that by investing $100 every month from the ages of 25 to 65 into an account with a 12% yield, Gen Z could retire with around $1,188,342. A millennial who started their investment journey just five years later, at age 30, would accumulate around $649,626 by age 65, she warned.

Recent findings suggest that “With a 12% annual average rate of return—the markets can do that for you—you’d have a million dollars,” she explained. “If there’s anything the younger generation needs to understand, it’s that the key ingredient to any financial freedom recipe is compounding.”.

Are you still working in retirement, or planning to? Get in touch: orianna.royle@fortune.com.

Lawmakers form bipartisan caucus to create meaningful AI safety legislation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers remarked today they’re forming a fresh AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.
  • It has been revealed that the lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks.
  • Industry observers note that these incidents have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” remarked Representative George Whitesides (D-California), a co-chair of the caucus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:48 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers remarked today they’re forming a fresh AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.

It has been revealed that the lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks. They also pointed to another incident involving the now-public Anthropic PBC, which also reported that its agents escaped their testing environments to access third-party systems.

Industry observers note that these incidents have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” remarked Representative George Whitesides (D-California), a co-chair of the caucus. “As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems and threats to national security.”.

Recent findings suggest that whitesides (pictured) is co-chairing the caucus alongside Representatives Nathanial Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia). In a post on X, they stressed the need for bipartisan collaboration to create the basic policy guardrails for AI safety, citing the growing concerns of the American public.

According to recent reports, does it feel like there's a fresh tech or AI crisis every day? Recent headlines are raising serious concerns about our digital safety and security.

Today, I'm joining @RepDonBeyer, @RepNateMoran, and over 20 of our colleagues to launch the bipartisan AI Safety and Innovation… pic.twitter.com/bhMyygy1J6.

Sources indicate that — Rep. George Whitesides (@Rep_Whitesides) November 19, 2026.

The 26-member caucus includes seven Republicans, which is a surprising number given that the White House administration under President Donald Trump has strongly opposed any heavy-handed regulation of the AI industry. The goal of the caucus is to identify “targeted solutions” that ensure AI remains under control without derailing innovation and threatening America’s lead in the industry.

Whitesides said the lawmakers will focus on two things: proposing legislation to augment AI safety, and responding rapidly to high-profile security incidents by gathering developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and come up with solutions.

“We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides told Politico in an interview. He said the group will work together to propose, provide feedback and endorse fresh AI legislation. He believes there’s an urgent need for this, because most other groups within the House are more focused on educating members or creating legislation within their own parties, he said.

Another thing the caucus intends to do is to pursue relationships with outside AI experts who can help lawmakers to navigate complex policy decisions. It also wants to help raise public awareness around AI and its safety issues, and ensure members outside of relevant committees have the tools they need to contribute to new legislation and debate.

In the recent midterm elections, Americans made it clear that AI is becoming a major glitch for governance. Moreover, a recent survey revealed that 43% of Americans don’t trust either of the two major political parties to properly get a grip on AI safety, according to a one-pager that accompanied the press release.

According to recent reports, “Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan problem,” Moran said. “This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared.”.

#6123. Latest Update: Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

📖 Baca

Latest Update: Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:37 am.
  • Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.
  • The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:37 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software manufacturer, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

Industry observers note that his co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the firm filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health prepares that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Recent findings suggest that kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their aims “after we’ve built our product.”.

Industry observers note that but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Industry observers note that why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it indicates.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

Kelman, by his own account, is fresh to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend stated I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman mentioned the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

In a recent development, chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”.

The Sojourn site says the tech giant is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

Industry observers note that that fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

A new health blueprint typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the organization hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a latest mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He remarked at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Malicious JavaScript code snippets were planted on the websites of 178 organizations.

The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing consumers multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.

Report URI estimates that on November 16 the code sat in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets it crawled, and the real number is most likely higher.

Among the websites that could become victims of the hack are some of the largest names in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. BleepingComputer confirms that the script loads on many of them.

Industry observers note that essentially, the script's goal was to swap a wallet address on the page for the attacker's one, capture card numbers, take screenshots of pages and more. It was a whole stack of tools used to steal personal data, wallets and other assets.

According to recent reports, according to Report URI, the attacker's wallets received about $7,040 within the first nine hours. That is a drop in the ocean considering the names involved, though the losses from card skimming are unknown. A card skimmer was added later that day, and a hidden iframe tried to load an iOS exploit chain on older iPhones.

Industry observers note that optimizely confirmed that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to certain customer projects. How the flaw worked is yet to be confirmed.

If successful, it could become one of the largest supply-chain attacks we have ever witnessed. Considering the attack came from a third party, we might see one of the largest service migrations in the world, as none of the third-party services and libraries can be trusted nowadays if used through an API.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain tasks to third-party providers all the time, so witnessing a similar situation in our field is more than a possibility.

For product owners: stay cautious and rethink the use of services prone to exploits. For users: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

According to recent reports, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

The most notable words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division noted it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

In a recent development, it also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

According to recent reports, early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

Sources indicate that this is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to customers.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

According to recent reports, A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the concerns presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

It has been revealed that in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

In a recent development, for a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

In a recent development, the framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

According to recent reports, the two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

In a recent development, that sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

Recent findings suggest that the harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

It has been revealed that for now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After decades of playing a doctor on the long-running medical drama ER and today’s The Pitt, Noah Wyle has learned a thing or two about what it’s like to be a health care professional and the challenges patients face.

Now, he is taking that passion off-screen, partnering up with popular scrubs maker FIGS with a goal to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt in the U.S.

“In my countless interactions with healthcare professionals over the decades, one thing that stays with me is how they try to do everything right for a patient while the system makes it harder than it should be,” Wyle stated in a statement. “Medical debt follows people home, creates long-term devastation, and changes the whole experience of care.”.

Americans owe at least $220 billion in medical debt, according to a 2024 KFF-Peterson analysis of federal survey data, and having insurance offers less protection than many assume. In a latest Urban Institute study backed by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, more than one-quarter of U.S. adults said they or a family member owed medical debt at the end of 2025, including 26% of those with health coverage. Hospitals were the most common creditor.

Separately, a Commonwealth Fund survey released in September found that roughly one in three working-age adults with private insurance are paying off medical bills over time, with some pulling from savings or spending less on food and rent to keep up. The problem has also come up on screen in Wyle’s reveals. In one episode of The Pitt, a construction worker who already owes $100,000 in medical bills lands in the ER with serious diabetes complications after rationing his insulin because he can’t afford it.

“Trust is the bedrock of the relationship between patients and clinicians like nurses, pharmacists and doctors and that trust is increasingly undermined by the burden, and even fear, of medical debt,” Allison Sesso, CEO and president of nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, said in a statement.

In a recent development, during the next three years, Wyle and FIGS will each donate $1 million to Undue Medical Debt, which wipes out, on average, $100 of qualifying medical debt for every $1 donated. The commitment is projected to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt for over 150,000 Americans. The first round of relief is set to take place in time for the upcoming holidays, according to the release.

Recent findings suggest that wyle, FIGS, and Undue Medical Debt over the same time frame will work to develop and share practical resources for health care professionals to help patients navigate affordability. This builds on FIGS’ and Wyle’s broader “Healthcare is Human” advocacy work, focused on addressing systemic pressures making it challenging for health care workers to care for their patients.

“This is an act of half philanthropy, and half protest, to underscore what the need is, and see if we can’t get our arms around some better solutions,” Wyle told CNN.

Industry observers note that wyle also serves as FIGS’ global brand ambassador and has joined the manufacturer on Capitol Hill to push for policies supporting health care workers. He also wore the brand’s first black-tie scrubs to the Emmys last year.

FIGS, a publicly traded manufacturer cofounded by CEO Trina Spear, reported third-quarter revenue of $190.7 million earlier this month, up nearly 26% from a year earlier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

Recent findings suggest that enhancement, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA stated Tuesday.

Industry observers note that in its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA mentioned it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA stated. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

Industry observers note that ULA noted Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based organization hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and Fresh Glenn for our return to flight.”.

Sources indicate that impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Newly introduced Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller noted before the flight.

Recent findings suggest that before Sunday, Amazon had introduced 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

According to recent reports, amazon has said it intends to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

HSP-029 was written by Sal Ternullo, CEO of SVRN, and opened for forum discussion on Oct. 7. The vote closed on Nov. 2, and 99.96% of the veNEAR cast was in favor of the proposal; no veNEAR was cast against it. The Security Council's 14-day window to veto the proposal closed on Nov. 16 with no veto, according to House of Stake.

According to recent reports, this is the second inflation cut for NEAR in just over a year. In October 2025, the maximum issuance was halved from the original 5% to 2.5%, and in September 2026, the realized issuance stood at 2.45%, according to HSP-029.

At 1.6%, NEAR will have "one of the lowest annual issuance rates among major blockchains," House of Stake remarked.

Industry observers note that according to House of Stake, the reduction will start one quarter after ratification, and validators still have to adopt the protocol upgrade. The issuance cap will reach 1.6% after 24 months.

Recent findings suggest that ternullo estimated in HSP-029 that NEAR will avoid issuing 11.8 million tokens over two years. At the current price, these tokens would be worth around $38.5 million.

It has been revealed that the proposal also calculated that the staking yield of NEAR will go down from around 5.27% to around 3.37% if the staking ratio stays the same. More than half of all NEAR is not staked, according to House of Stake.

Industry observers note that bitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes recently named NEAR among four tokens that he expects to rise before the end of the AI bubble. Hayes set targets of $6 for NEAR, $2,800 for ETH, $1,800 for ZEC, and $40 for VVV.

#6116. If Your Business Can’t Run Without You, You Have a Bigger Problem Than You Think

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1309 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

If Your Business Can’t Run Without You, You Have a Bigger Problem Than You Think

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business.
  • According to recent reports, A client needs an update.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

According to recent reports, A client needs an update. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

One lesson I’ve learned is that being needed and being effective are not always the same thing. And for entrepreneurs, recognizing that difference can change how a firm grows.

In the beginning, founders have to do almost everything.

You win the business, manage customers, handle finances and solve problems because there isn’t anyone else. You know where everything stands. You remember the commitments you’ve made. You understand why certain decisions were taken.

Industry observers note that that knowledge becomes an advantage. But as your manufacturer grows, it can also become a problem.

Industry observers note that employees get accustomed to asking you because you know the answer. Customers prefer speaking directly with you because you’ve always been available. And gradually, even decisions that should be made elsewhere find their way back to your desk.

The strange part is that this can feel rewarding. Being the person everyone needs reinforces the belief that you’re essential to the company’s success.

But ask yourself something uncomfortable: If the business requires your involvement in nearly every decision, have you actually built an organization, or have you simply created a more demanding job?

Industry observers note that I’ve seen business owners respond to overwhelming workloads by hiring additional employees. Sometimes that’s exactly what the business needs. But adding people doesn’t automatically reduce the founder’s workload.

It has been revealed that if nobody has the authority to make decisions, additional employees may simply create additional questions. I previously explored this problem in an Entrepreneur article about examining workflows before hiring.

The underlying concern is often less about headcount and more about how work moves through an organization.

Consider a project manager who is responsible for delivering a client project but needs the founder’s approval for every minor adjustment. Technically, the project has been delegated. In reality, the founder is still managing it.

The project manager has responsibility without sufficient authority, and that creates frustration on both sides. Delegation only works when people know which decisions they can make independently, what boundaries apply and when something genuinely needs to be escalated.

This is the part of leadership that requires some self-reflection. It’s easy to complain that employees keep asking questions. It’s harder to recognize that our own behavior may have encouraged it.

Sources indicate that if a manager makes a reasonable decision and we immediately reverse it, we’re teaching that person to seek approval next time. If we insist on reviewing every email, presentation and customer response, we’re communicating that we don’t trust others to exercise judgment. And if we consistently step in to solve problems before employees have a chance to work through them, we’re reinforcing the very dependency we want to eliminate.

I’ve learned that people need room to make decisions, including decisions that may not be exactly the ones I would have made. That doesn’t mean lowering standards. It means being clear about the result you expect while allowing capable employees to determine how to achieve it.

In a recent development, A team doesn’t become independent because the founder unveils that everyone should take more ownership. Independence develops when people are genuinely given the opportunity to exercise it.

One aspect of running a business that doesn’t receive enough attention is the mental burden of keeping everything moving.

According to recent reports, you may delegate the preparation of a report, but still be the person remembering when it’s due. You may assign someone to manage a client, but still feel responsible for anticipating every glitch that could arise. You may have a team handling operations while remaining the person mentally tracking every unresolved problem.

According to recent reports, the work has been distributed, but the responsibility hasn’t. This distinction reminds me of the concept of the mental load, often discussed in the context of family responsibilities and working mothers.

The same principle applies to leadership. There’s a difference between completing a task and being responsible for remembering, organizing and following through on everything associated with it.

If a founder continues carrying all of that responsibility, delegation may provide temporary relief without changing the underlying problem. True ownership means someone else is accountable for both the task and the outcome.

I would encourage entrepreneurs to run a simple experiment.

It has been revealed that choose five business days when you deliberately step away from routine operational decisions. You don’t need to disappear completely. Remain available for genuine emergencies and decisions involving significant financial, legal or reputational risk. But resist the temptation to intervene in every ordinary problem.

It has been revealed that before the experiment begins, clarify who owns each function and what decisions they can make. Then pay attention to what happens.

Do projects continue moving? Can customers get answers? Are managers comfortable making decisions? Where does work stall? More importantly, why?

According to recent reports, perhaps employees lack access to information. Maybe approval limits are unclear. Or perhaps certain processes exist only in your head. Those are the concerns worth fixing.

When the five days are over, review the decisions your team handled successfully alongside the problems they encountered.

Sources indicate that don’t use the exercise to identify who failed. Use it to understand where the business remains unnecessarily dependent on you.

Entrepreneurs often associate growth with more customers, higher revenue and larger teams. Those are key measures.

But I would add another: How much can your business accomplish without requiring the founder to supervise every detail?

This doesn’t mean becoming disconnected from your company. A founder should remain closely involved in strategy, major relationships and decisions that shape the future of the business. But there’s a difference between leading an organization and personally keeping every part of it functioning.

As you plan the next stage of growth, look beyond what your business is accomplishing and examine how it’s accomplishing it.

Industry observers note that are you developing leaders who can make sound decisions? Have you created processes that survive someone’s absence? Can your team solve problems without waiting for you? If not, you may have a business that’s growing in size without growing in capability.

Here’s the challenge I’d leave every entrepreneur with: Take five working days away from routine decisions and see what breaks.

Industry observers note that whatever stops working deserves your attention when you return. Because the goal of building a business shouldn’t be to make yourself indispensable forever. It should be to build something strong enough that you don’t have to be.

Industry observers note that there’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

A client needs an patch. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

The November news cycle has fixated on elections, Nvidia, and Anthropic, but the Iran war has quietly escalated this week and there is no “credible pathway” for the world to return to its previous norm, the International Energy Agency warned in its annual World Energy Outlook released Thursday.

According to recent reports, even as gasoline and diesel prices have fallen from record highs in recent weeks, the Middle East will never be the same and the rest of the world is still racing to develop more of its own energy sources—both renewables and fossil fuels—as global supplies remain tight and food security is threatened in much of the world, especially Asia, the report stated. All this is transpiring as global energy demand spikes both from the AI boom and the rise of the middle class in developing countries.

In a recent development, “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” stated IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

Recent findings suggest that the nearly nine-month Iran war and the prolonged shuttering of the vital Strait of Hormuz represent the greatest energy supply shock in modern history—far more than the Iranian Revolution or the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s—and its reverberations will be felt in ways that remain unclear, the report said. After all, the war is ongoing and Iran this week struck U.S. facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the U.S. countered by striking Iran’s Qeshm Island.

Sources indicate that “Attention is elsewhere now. I don’t know if it’s complacency or a lack of anxiety, but [the war] is still a pretty substantial deal,” said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm.

According to recent reports, “What I worry is if the Iranians feel they have to make people anxious again? Do they view it in their strategic interest to create more anxiety?” Pickering told Fortune. “I think we’ll have this uneasy conflict going on with Iran for a bunch of 2027.”.

Between alternative pipelines and routes, and U.S. escorts through Hormuz, Middle Eastern oil exports are approaching 90% of their pre-war levels despite the ongoing military strikes, said Pavel Molchanov, Raymond James energy analyst. “This indicates that the oil market has become acclimated to periodic flareups, just as long as there is no return to all-out war,” he added. “That said, the lack of a U.S.-Iran deal still translates into a hefty risk premium.”.

It has been revealed that because of seasonal demand dips, rising Middle Eastern exports, and President Donald Trump’s emphasis on deescalating the war since the midterm congressional elections, global oil prices have fallen below the $100 per barrel threshold, even though the global benchmark remains high at more than $90. After all, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is dangerously depleted at a 44-year low and the world has cumulatively lost 2.8 billion barrels of oil over nearly nine months, the IEA report stated.

It has been revealed that the Iran war has triggered record-high fuel spikes in the U.S. But keep in mind that the U.S. leads the world in oil output, at the moment producing an all-time high of more than 14 million barrels daily. The rest of the world is left even more at the mercy of the war, and its price spikes and physical shortages are amplified, especially in Asia and Africa.

More than 4 billion people—roughly half of the global population—depended on the Middle East for over 30% of its oil supplies. And about 80% of Middle Eastern oil exports were destined for Asia before the war.

Even as Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Iraq move to build pipelines to divert oil supplies through alternate routes, those projects will take years, and long-term Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz would maintain uncertainty going forward.

It has been revealed that “That’s not a particularly comforting outlook to the consumers of Middle East crude,” Pickering noted. “The finish matters, and I don’t think we have visibility on what the finish looks like.”.

The Americas are leading the increase in oil production—the U.S., Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Guyana, and now Venezuela—as well as a slate of African nations. And more countries are investing in renewable energy and electrification for electric vehicles.

Industry observers note that birol and the IEA forecast that renewables—solar, wind, and batteries—are picking up momentum throughout the world even as the globe falls short of its climate change goals. Nuclear power also is gaining steam. EV sales are projected to rise in most of the world next year—less so in the U.S.—in part because of cheaper, subsidized Chinese EVs being exported worldwide.

Sources indicate that global oil demand is now expected to peak by 2030 and slowly decline from there, the IEA remarked. Natural gas demand will grow through the mid-2030s and plateau.

The IEA outlook noted that August was the hottest month ever on record worldwide and a strong El Niño could add to weather-related strains heading into 2027. “High energy prices and shortfalls in fertilizer supply are creating hazards for food security,” the report stated. “Emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) and air pollutants from fuel combustion remain dangerously high. Energy geopolitics are fracturing, and trade restrictions are on the rise. Trust is in short supply. Each vulnerability deepens the others.”.

That is why—more than ever—the world requires “credible roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels, backed by the public finance needed to ensure a fast and fair transition,” mentioned David Tong, global industry lead at Oil Change International.

According to recent reports, “Fossil fuels are driving chaos and high energy bills, and the energy choices we make now will shape all our futures,” Tong added. “After yet another fossil fuel crisis, governments cannot afford to keep people and economies hooked on volatile oil and gas markets.”.

Along these lines, Ledger confirmed that its team had remediated the concern and that the malicious code was no longer being served through its website.

Ledger emphasizes that the incident did not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices and that user private keys remain protected by their Ledger device, thus reassuring consumers that the incident had not compromised the core security of its wallet products.

According to researcher Scott Helme, on November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organizations' websites across several sectors through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform. The websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger, and Peacock.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed, with only 1 of the 188 infected snippets found, down from 169.

According to recent reports, the main point is that trusted JavaScript is not always trustworthy. A third-party dependency can exploit a website without ever breaking the website's own code or infrastructure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, what does a Reddit search ad have to do with the creator economy? More than it first appears. When someone looks up a gaming headset or asks which software is worth paying for, Reddit wants to be more than the place where people discuss the options. It is testing ads alongside search results, putting promotions close to a high-intent decision.

It has been revealed that that move makes more sense when you look at the conversations Reddit is selling access to. The firm points advertisers to its 1,300 gaming communities and cites TransUnion research finding that 71% of U.S. Reddit gamers had purchased a gaming product based on information they found on the platform.

It is a platform-sponsored finding, not a forecast for every campaign. Still, it demonstrates why community context can be more valuable than a broad audience count: The discussion may already be helping someone decide.

Reddit is building out that decision path inside its product. In a test, AI-powered product discovery can summarize community discussions, show product information and send shoppers to a retailer. A user could ask for recommendations, compare what Redditors say and move toward a product without starting over somewhere else.

Industry observers note that there is a business reason to make that journey shorter. Reddit’s ad revenue climbed 54% in the third quarter of 2026. Yet the company also faces a vulnerability: In October, its CEO noted search referrals fell by more than a million a week on average, citing changes to Google’s AI search experience. Building a destination people use directly is one way to reduce reliance on another company’s results page.

Reddit’s AI strategy has another side. The platform has given Google structured access to Reddit content and formed a partnership with OpenAI, while developing its own AI search and shopping tools. Those moves create a tension: The same discussions can help answer a question in another product, attract an ad on Reddit or lead to a product listing on Reddit. Who gets the value from that recommendation is becoming a business question, not just a product question.

According to recent reports, the pattern extends well beyond Reddit. On YouTube, creator partnerships and shopping connect brand discovery, sponsored videos, product tags and affiliate income. Pinterest is making it easier for creators to connect storefronts to product pins. Google is also testing ads in AI Mode, bringing sponsored offers into conversational search. Each manufacturer starts with a different strength, whether it is video, visual inspiration, search or community. All are trying to connect influence to action with fewer steps in between.

Industry observers note that this is a bigger definition of the creator economy. It includes the creator, but also the system around that person: discovery tools that match a brand to a voice, paid distribution that extends a post’s reach, shopping features that monetize a recommendation and AI that helps a customer make sense of it. Communities can play a similar role even when there is no single influencer at the center.

According to recent reports, for brands, a shorter path from recommendation to purchase can make campaigns easier to run and measure. The trade-off is that a platform may control the audience data, the recommendation, the ad placement and the definition of success. Creators face a similar bargain. Newly introduced tools can open income streams, but access depends on platform rules, algorithms and fees. And the communities whose conversations influence a purchase may not share in the value those conversations create.

I have seen this kind of shift before. Search began as another channel to test; the companies that moved early understood it was infrastructure for existing demand. Discovery is changing again. People can use AI search and Google during the same research process, then look for a creator’s review or a community’s experience. That overlap makes it harder to assign one channel all the credit, but it does not make each influence less notable.

For a brand, the competition is often for the moment before purchase, when someone decides which options deserve a closer look. The platform that earns that moment can shape the shortlist long before a customer reaches a checkout page.

Industry observers note that begin with the facts an AI assistant, creator or customer might use to describe your business. Product details, pricing, availability, policies and differentiators should be accurate wherever they appear. Strong third-party coverage, credible reviews and useful customer experiences give people evidence to evaluate. A paid placement cannot compensate for conflicting claims or stale information.

Then plan around context, not just audience size. A creator’s expertise or a community’s product knowledge may matter most when someone is comparing options. Paid media, communications, creator partnerships, search and ecommerce teams should be working from the same view of that journey.

Measurement needs the same broader lens. Track AI mentions, branded searches, qualified leads and sales alongside creator and community activity. Ask customers what helped them decide. Platform reporting is useful, but compare it with your own results instead of assuming a view or click tells the whole story. Building AI search visibility is part of that work, not a substitute for measuring whether the right customers act.

Sources indicate that finally, give people a reason to keep the relationship going beyond the platform: useful product information, a strong site experience, an email program or a customer community. The goal is not to avoid platform commerce. It is to benefit from the upcoming routes to discovery without making one company the only place your brand can be found, understood or purchased.

According to recent reports, platforms are turning recommendations into a product. Brands that recognize the shift can earn a place in the decision, while keeping enough independence to understand what is working and why.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella remarked the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”.

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he stated. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”.

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

According to recent reports, it was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disney’s Sports segment posted $4.6 billion in revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter, up 16% from a year earlier, while operating income jumped 53%.
  • 44 on the 2026 Fortune 500, is raising its content budget, with sports rights a major line item, while trimming the rest of the manufacturer to fund growth.
  • It has been revealed that ESPN offers something most streaming libraries can’t: appointment viewing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For now, the bet is paying off. Disney’s Sports segment posted $4.6 billion in revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter, up 16% from a year earlier, while operating income jumped 53%. But Disney is pairing that push with a blueprint to cut about $3 billion in annual costs by fiscal 2029, signaling how far it is moving away from the traditional TV business that once paid for everything.

That tension defines the strategy. Disney, No. 44 on the 2026 Fortune 500, is raising its content budget, with sports rights a major line item, while trimming the rest of the manufacturer to fund growth.

It has been revealed that ESPN offers something most streaming libraries can’t: appointment viewing. Fans watch live, in large numbers, and advertisers pay a premium to reach them.

It has been revealed that disney deepened that advantage in January, when ESPN closed its acquisition of NFL Network and NFL Fantasy, along with the rights to distribute the RedZone channel to cable and satellite operators. In exchange, the NFL took a 10% stake in ESPN. Disney now holds an effective 72% interest in the network, according to its fiscal fourth-quarter shareholder letter, and Hearst owns 18%.

Audiences are rewarding the bet. Monday Night Football drew its best Week 1 and Week 2 audiences ever this season. ABC’s September broadcast of Ohio State vs. Texas pulled in about 14 million viewers, ESPN’s most-watched regular-season college football game in a decade.

College football is the backbone. In November, ESPN secured exclusive rights to the expanded 24-team College Football Playoff beginning in the 2027-28 season. The upcoming format grows the postseason from 11 games to 23, and the deal runs through the 2031-32 season.

The direction is clear: Disney wants sports woven into its global streaming business, not walled off inside a cable package.

Recent findings suggest that the quarter’s numbers explain the appeal. Sports subscription and affiliate fee revenue rose 18%, and advertising revenue grew 20%.

Industry observers note that those growth rates come with caveats. Disney’s fiscal 2026 ran 53 weeks, and the extra week landed in the fourth quarter. The comparison was also easier: a year earlier, ESPN was spending heavily to market the launch of its Unlimited streaming service.

Premium rights are not cheap. The Sports segment’s costs and expenses rose 5% in the quarter, to $3.2 billion, partly reflecting contractual rate increases and costs associated with new sports rights. Disney expects to spend about $26 billion on content in fiscal 2027, roughly 9% more than this year, including more sports rights and international programming.

In a recent development, CFO Hugh Johnston has argued that the biggest bills are already known. “In terms of sports rights, we’re actually pretty well locked up through 2029 or 2030,” he told a Goldman Sachs conference in September, adding that Disney had passed on Formula 1 because it had become too expensive.

In a recent development, not everyone thinks sports can carry a streaming business. “At the end of the day, all these streamers and platforms have to keep putting new stuff on screens, and sports isn’t going to solve the need for 75% of viewership,” Alex Iosilevich, co-founder of media, entertainment, and gaming investment firm Alignment Growth, told Business Insider in 2024.

Disney is targeting about $3 billion in annual run-rate operating expense savings by fiscal 2029. The program has already included several rounds of layoffs this year affecting thousands of employees, and more cuts are expected. Johnston said savings will also come from technology and real estate consolidation, with shared services another opportunity.

According to recent reports, CEO Josh D’Amaro, who succeeded Bob Iger in March, acknowledged the toll. “Changes like these are not easy,” he said, calling them “important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment.”.

The savings are not simply a war chest for rights fees. Disney says the money will primarily fund future growth, including streaming, with a portion reaching the bottom line over time. D’Amaro has also pushed to make Disney+ the company’s front door; executives have reportedly discussed a “super app” that would fold park tickets, merchandise, and cruise bookings into the streaming service.

None of this means Disney is abandoning movies, television, or its franchises. It is changing where the money goes as traditional television faces mounting pressure.

But the full ESPN lineup still sits behind separate subscriptions, and the week’s biggest college football games have largely stayed off the Disney+ simulcast schedule. That leaves viewers sorting out which events come with which blueprint.

Disney is betting that live sports can draw audiences, strengthen its streaming business, and command premium ad rates. The test is whether it can make that spending pay without pushing subscription prices past what consumers will tolerate. The first major reading comes Feb. 14; the next arrives when the 24-team playoff kicks off in December 2027.

  • Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club revealed Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a latest job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club revealed Tuesday.

In a recent development, “His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer remarked in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”.

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation organization toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew remarked his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”.

It has been revealed that chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he noted. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

In a recent development, the couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew noted.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he mentioned.

Industry observers note that talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew indicates he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”.

Chew is also working with players.

In a recent development, he recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew noted. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

Industry observers note that “It has to be approachable for folks,” he remarked. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”.

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he remarked.

ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • According to recent reports, headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

According to recent reports, headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

In a recent development, that detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no latest mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Recent findings suggest that governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain claims nothing moves unless it passes.

Sources indicate that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's newly introduced private AI app, ZetaLabs, introduces alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

It has been revealed that the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

It has been revealed that holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

Recent findings suggest that on Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

In a recent development, that sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain states it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain notes the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

It has been revealed that on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain indicates it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement blueprint for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.
