💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bananas are one of the cheapest groceries at supermarkets.
  • Less rainfall stunts bananas’ growth, which can yield harvest losses of up to 65%, and too much rainfall waterlogs the soil and incubates fungal and bacterial disease, which also reduces yields.
  • Recent findings suggest that the threat is part of why growers are asking wholesalers for more money for the fruit—and getting it—which could test bananas’ status as a loss leader for grocery stores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bananas are one of the cheapest groceries at supermarkets. Americans paid just 66 cents per pound of the yellow fruit in October, compared to $2.10 for tomatoes and $2.14 for lemons, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data. But they’re about to get more expensive thanks to El Niño, which causes either wetter-or-drier-than-usual conditions for banana growers thousands of miles away.

Less rainfall stunts bananas’ growth, which can yield harvest losses of up to 65%, and too much rainfall waterlogs the soil and incubates fungal and bacterial disease, which also reduces yields. And this year’s El Niño could be historically destructive, with about a 60% chance of the event exceeding previous El Niños dating back to 1950.

Recent findings suggest that the threat is part of why growers are asking wholesalers for more money for the fruit—and getting it—which could test bananas’ status as a loss leader for grocery stores. Costa Rica’s National Banana Corporation has recommended increasing the minimum export price of bananas by nearly 10% for next year, citing climate-driven productivity losses, a stronger currency and higher costs after seven years of no changes. Fairtrade International also approved a 5.6% increase in its average minimum prices for banana growers starting in January, citing El Niño as one of the reasons.

Francisco Martin-Rayo, CEO and cofounder of agricultural commodity price and climate risk forecaster Helios AI, told Fortune the El Niño weather extremes are “dramatically higher” and could destroy harvests next year.

According to recent reports, “A lot of harvests will be ruined, 1,000%,” Martin-Rayo mentioned. “We worry about this dramatically for 2027.”.

It has been revealed that the world’s top banana exporter Ecuador has already recorded 851 floods between Aug. 29 and Nov. 13, with banana-growing provinces Guayas, Los Ríos, and El Oro among those affected, and has issued a red alert for El Niño. According to a report Helios shared with Fortune, Ecuador is experiencing climate stress that is four times its historical level for this time of year because of heavy rainfall, and other top banana exporters Costa Rica and the Philippines are facing similar stress.

“It is way too wet for bananas being grown in Ecuador and Costa Rica right now, and it is way too hot for bananas being grown in the Philippines right now, and so that means you’re going to have production and yield impacts,” Martin-Rayo noted.

In a recent development, in the U.S., the cost of importing bananas has also climbed because of the Iran war pushing  up diesel and fertilizer prices. During the first five months of 2026, banana imports rose 3% by volume but 12% by value compared with the same period last year, according to Department of Agriculture data.

Still, higher costs don’t necessarily mean higher prices for shoppers. Rob Weston, the founder of agricultural data analytics firm CropGPT, told Fortune that grocery stores have typically absorbed the costs when selling bananas.

“Bananas are interesting because grocery stores globally have traditionally treated them as loss leaders to attract shoppers, keeping retail margins extremely low and passing the financial burden directly down the supply chain to growers,” Weston stated.

But Martin-Rayo mentioned while price hikes are unlikely in the short term, he expects at least some in the long term because of El Niño, though he’s unsure exactly when they’ll manifest on store shelves.

“We’re already seeing this wholesale crisis, but the question is at what point does the retailer decide to pass those price increases through to the consumer,” Martin-Rayo stated.

According to recent reports, seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

It has been revealed that the department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD said in a blog post last week.

It has been revealed that it’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

SPD also spelled out what Spot won’t do.

According to recent reports, the robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD noted a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

Industry observers note that the only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”.

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

In a recent development, nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Spot appears decidedly less cuddly.

In a recent development, boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the tech giant’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

In a recent development, police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD noted, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”.

Industry News: From losing it all to a $1 billion valuation: How Motorway’s CEO bounced back from failure

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak.
  • “We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune.
  • In a recent development, their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak. Together, they built and sold office space platform Officila Space, broadband comparison site Top10.com, and LoanCube, a lead-generation site that was sold for $1 million.

“We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune. “And then we got quite schooled.”.

In a recent development, their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital. It grew promptly, until Booking.com and the major hotel chains caught developed their own mobile apps. “All of the big hotel brands got mobile and killed us,” Leathes said.

The founders spent two years trying to rescue the business, and a sale fell through at the last minute. They shut it down in 2015. “We lost all the money for the investors,” he said, referring to the $12.4 million the company had raised from backers including Balderton Capital and Accel. “We had to let go of the whole team.” The startup had 14 employees in London when it raised its last round in 2014.

It was a “tough lesson,” Leathes admitted. The three went their separate ways, but within six months they were back together. “We had unfinished business,” he said. Their next venture, the trio agreed, had to be “the substantial one—the manufacturer that we can do for the next 10 or 20 years.”.

It has been revealed that leathes, Jones, and Buttle set about developing their next business idea from a disused hospital in Camden, north London, that was scheduled to be demolished. A charity had taken over the lease and was renting out the abandoned wards to startups as cheap office space. “All this medical stuff was everywhere,” Leathes recalled, and meetings were held in the old operating theater.

Their fifth business idea proved more successful. Motorway, an online marketplace for used cars, was valued at $1 billion in 2001, following a $190 million funding round co-led by Index Ventures and Iconiq. Its 2025 revenue rose 18% to £78 million ($99 million), and its operating losses fell by more than a third to about £22 million ($28 million). Leathes notes the company is on track to make its first profit in 2026.

In a recent development, “We learned a massive amount, both through all the companies that had worked, but also the ones that didn’t,” Leathes said. “Those lessons helped us make a lot of the right decisions as we scaled Motorway.”.

Reflecting on the failure of his hotel recommendation app, Leathes noted: “What we built wasn’t differentiated enough. If you want to take on Booking.com or Expedia, then you need to rethink the market and build Airbnb, not just a better version of what’s already out there.”.

With Motorway, the three cofounders took a different approach. By building a marketplace that connects private sellers directly with dealers they were able to cut out the middlemen, Leathes mentioned. The car trade “a bit of a graveyard of tech companies coming in thinking they could change it,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that the best-known casualty, online car retailer Cazoo, went public in 2021. It spent heavily on marketing and expansion, then collapsed into administration in 2024.

Motorway took the opposite approach. “We cold-called dealers, stitched deals together on WhatsApp and spent much of our time driving around the country meeting [them],” Leathes stated. “That’s how we learned the trade. That’s what taught us what we needed to build.”.

Industry observers note that those early months taught him to let customers shape the business. “It’s the early customers that form the product,” he said. “That means holding the original idea quite lightly and being really willing to drop things that you feel passionate about.” Founders, he added, often need to “pivot really aggressively.”.

Sources indicate that the other lesson was focus. When COVID-19 lockdowns shut Britain’s physical car auctions, dealers flocked to Motorway. The founders raised fresh capital to scale the core business rather than chase upcoming markets. “If you have something that’s really working, triple down on it,” Leathes stated. Nearly a decade in, Motorway still operates only in the UK, although its long-term goal is global expansion.

Sources indicate that leathes mentioned Motorway is open to an IPO but there are no immediate prepares. What’s more, London may not be its first choice of listing venue. “At the moment it’s not attractive to scale-ups,” he said. Just eight companies listed in the U.K. in the first nine months of 2026, according to accounting firm EY.

In Europe, Germany’s Auto1, which also buys cars from private sellers and sells them on to dealers, listed in Frankfurt in 2021. Leathes believes a London float by a homegrown star such as Revolut or Monzo “would definitely help” revive the U.K.’s lackluster market.

But the bar for going public is also shifting. Leathes pointed to the AI boom, led by Anthropic, which this week raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO on record. “This is drastically changing what good looks like in public tech companies,” he noted. Investors now measure listings against AI companies growing at extraordinary speed and scale, which makes steady, near-profitable businesses a harder sell.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm.

It has been revealed that microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” mentioned Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the manufacturer’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

Sources indicate that the full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou noted.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” consumers of each company’s agent tools, it highlighted $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

In a recent development, partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced latest Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The manufacturer is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

According to recent reports, the companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly customers as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

Latest MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

Sources indicate that the lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft claims it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it indicates matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

In a recent development, the other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Organization consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff highlighted Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

According to recent reports, the cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A newly introduced Agent 365 Business Analytics feature indicates business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

  • Like clockwork, the digital marketing echo chamber sounds the death knell every few years: “SEO is dead.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Like clockwork, the digital marketing echo chamber sounds the death knell every few years: “SEO is dead.”.

I entered this game in the early 2000s as a web developer. I was building sites at night while working a full-time job during the day. If I wanted traffic, I had to figure out search engine optimization through trial and error.

My first transactional store lived on Yahoo! Stores, selling generic mini MP3 players — that is, until the iPod wiped that category out overnight. Next, I sold GPS navigation software on CDs, which stopped when the iPhone made standalone navigation devices obsolete.

Then came an ecommerce brand called Soccer Nation. Growth happened fast. We opened a physical storefront in Vista, California, at the same time that David Beckham signed with the LA Galaxy of the MLS, and watched revenue climb for years. Then the 2008 recession froze retail spending. We shuttered the retail shop and sold the domain to a competitor who turned it into an online soccer publication.

Recent findings suggest that this is key because I’ve spent more than two decades watching technological and economic disruptions dismantle business models. Every time Google rolled out a major algorithm upgrade — Panda, Penguin, Hummingbird, Helpful Content — the same panic ensued. Marketers declared that search was finished. I pushed back each time with: “SEO isn’t dead. It’s just evolving.”.

This time, however, the underlying shift is fundamentally different from anything we’ve seen over the past 25 years.

Recent findings suggest that in prior cycles, the rules changed, but the referee stayed the same. Google updated its algorithms, penalized black-hat tactics and forced brands to create better experiences. Through it all, Mountain View remained the undisputed gatekeeper of the internet.

Google isn’t just updating the rules this time. It is losing its monopoly over human intent.

Discovery is decentralizing. Consumers no longer instinctively open a browser window, navigate to a search bar and wade through ten blue links buried beneath four sponsored ads. Instead, discovery happens natively where consumers live, via ambient operating systems, vertical AI engines and conversational interfaces.

Take my own household as a real-world case study:.

I genuinely can’t remember anyone in my family running a standard Google search.

This behavioral pivot is driving massive market shifts. Tech market corrections and capital reallocations, such as Alphabet shedding hundreds of billions in market cap during major competitive platform announcements, are not anomalies. They are a lagging indicator of a structural reality: Google’s absolute control over the web’s front door has permanently fractured.

As user behavior shifts from rigid keywords (“best running shoes flat feet”) to complex, conversational prompts (“Compare the top stability running shoes for wide, flat feet under $200 with solid arch support for marathon prep”), standard keyword density and thin programmatic landing pages fail completely.

Enter Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), also referred to as Generative Engine Optimization (GEO).

If your marketing leadership is still treating AEO as a minor technical checklist item — uploading an llms.txt file, structuring basic JSON-LD schema and tweaking H2s to question formats — you are missing the forest for the trees.

Winning citation share inside modern language models demands an integrated on-page and off-page architecture built around four core pillars:.

It has been revealed that large language models prioritize information efficiency. Models bypass content that regurgitates commodity definitions. Winning content provides primary data, original research, proprietary case studies and clear, structured answers that an engine can cleanly ingest and quote without wading through filler.

LLMs operate on probabilistic associative networks and massive training corpora. If authoritative industry publications, trade journals and top-tier editorial outlets do not regularly cite your brand in direct association with your specific vertical, the model won’t know you exist. Instead, it will synthesize and recommend your competitors.

Answer engines heavily weigh verified public consensus. Unstructured discussions across Reddit, niche communities, review aggregators and professional directories serve as foundational data for conversational engines. Unmonitored reputation issues or a total absence from peer-to-peer discourse directly leads to exclusion from AI recommendations.

AEO requires managing how your brand is perceived across multiple distinct engines, such as Perplexity, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI. Because these systems ingest public social platforms to gauge real-time cultural relevance and expertise, your organic social footprint and executive thought leadership now directly fuel your search visibility.

SEO is not dead, but gone are the days of optimizing exclusively for a single search engine algorithm.

Sustainable organic visibility requires understanding how multi-modal models ingest, evaluate, synthesize and attribute authoritative sources across the entire open web. For entrepreneurs and executives planning growth initiatives, ensuring your business is cited, trusted and surfaced by generative answer engines is no longer an experimental line item. It is foundational to enterprise value.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

Sources indicate that A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

It has been revealed that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

Recent findings suggest that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It claims TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

Recent findings suggest that the card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

It has been revealed that here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Recent findings suggest that gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Sources indicate that against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card reveals the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

Industry observers note that the card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a significant generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 new tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Industry observers note that anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card indicates all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

The card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

Industry observers note that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday declared $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other developments.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners rapidly, is more vital than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason stated in a statement.

The firm combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

In a recent development, the latest round brings Aarden’s total funding to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he released the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” mentioned Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, stated the firm is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson remarked on LinkedIn.

For years, I thought I knew what separated my moving firm from others. I’m a fourth-generation mover and have worked in this industry professionally since I was 18. My father always stated moving was in my blood — hence our name, Can’t Quit Moving. I built my business on lessons passed down through my family: Work hard, treat people and their belongings with respect and do the job the right way. After hearing countless moving horror stories from customers, I knew we operated differently.

Industry observers note that and I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience. I certainly didn’t see our everyday work as content, as something other people would want to know more about or as something that could help grow the manufacturer. That changed when someone from outside the industry spent a day with us.

According to recent reports, during the pandemic, a good friend of mine who worked as a cameraman was out of work, so he joined our crew for a day. At the end of it, he climbed into the truck looking rattled. “That was a crazy day,” he told me. My response: “That was a Tuesday.”.

Recent findings suggest that every day, we dealt with closing delays, low bridges, furniture that wouldn’t fit, last-minute additions and customers navigating one of the most stressful days of their lives. To me, that was second nature. To him, it was a story, and he told me we needed to film it.

In a recent development, that eventually became an unscripted docuseries about our tech giant, but it also changed how I thought about growing a business. Until then, we had relied solely on word of mouth. What I hadn’t realized was that showing people what sets us apart from the competition could become a growth strategy.

When you spend every day doing the same thing, you lose sight of what makes it interesting. I didn’t think twice about the problems we encountered on a move, because solving them was my job. But to an outsider, the process was wild. Parking and loading our truck, for example, fascinated our cameraman. It made me realize that the work my team and I do takes real skill.

That’s something business owners in any industry can overlook. You don’t need a glamorous product or a business built for social media to have a story worth telling. A contractor solving a job site issue, a restaurant prepping for a Saturday night or a bookseller opening their store all have something customers rarely get to see.

Simply put, your best content could already be happening. You just have to recognize and document it.

When we started filming, I had to unlearn some of my business owner instincts. After our second day, my wife paused a piece of footage and asked what I had been thinking in that moment. The truth was, I had been thinking plenty. I just wasn’t saying it.

Sources indicate that I was trained to stay calm even when things went off the rails. My wife told me to talk to the camera like I was talking to my best friend. I had to rewire my thinking: Explain the problem. Share what you’re thinking. Admit when you’re frustrated. Just be real.

That taught me the difference between advertising and real storytelling. Business owners spend a lot of time telling customers who they are: We’re trustworthy. We care. We go above and beyond. And so on.

Sources indicate that documenting our work allowed us to show those things instead. Our motto is “We take the stress out of your move,” and now people could see that firsthand: how our crew wraps belongings to protect them from torrential rain, how we responded when a move didn’t go as planned because of an insurance headache and how we treated customers even when we were close to pulling our hair out under high-pressure deadlines. The messy moments revealed more about the manufacturer than the camera-ready ones.

Industry observers note that other entrepreneurs can learn from this. What do you claim about your business that you could demonstrate instead?

After we finished filming the show, a former customer who worked in the film industry encouraged us to start sharing our story on social media. Creating content consistently has sometimes felt like starting another business, but it also changed how I think about marketing. Traditional advertising usually tries to reach someone around the time they’re ready to buy. Telling a story and building an audience can create a relationship long before that.

That’s especially important in a business like moving. People don’t need movers every month. Someone might discover one of our videos today and not move for another year. But if they keep following the tech giant and seeing our crew at work, we don’t have to introduce ourselves when they’re finally ready for a quote. The audience comes first. The customer can come later.

And we’re starting to see that play out. When we ask newly introduced customers how they found us, more and more of them mention our videos. One man contacted us about moving his lemon trees because he’d seen us move palm trees on Instagram. During another move, a customer’s 6-year-old recognized us from our YouTube Shorts. To me, that was proof: People weren’t just remembering our moving organization. They were remembering us. They felt like they’d gotten to know the people behind the business, and more importantly, they already trusted us.

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

According to recent reports, the shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”.

According to recent reports, the change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

According to recent reports, muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

It has been revealed that for Muse people, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas noted any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

It has been revealed that what’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon mentioned it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Recent findings suggest that meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson mentioned the tech giant had nothing to share.

It has been revealed that amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

According to recent reports, the business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

It has been revealed that amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

Industry observers note that on Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy remarked outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

Breaking: Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

Recent findings suggest that according to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

According to recent reports, those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

It has been revealed that the sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

According to recent reports, timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

Recent findings suggest that this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

Industry observers note that app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Sources indicate that finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

It has been revealed that this is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams strategy to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

Industry observers note that the coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

It has been revealed that denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

Jeff Bezos claims Nvidia should look inside the tech giant for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

Industry observers note that “If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos remarked. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”.

Sources indicate that nvidia’s board indicates it has no aims to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the tech giant’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”.

Jones remarked the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place rapidly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He noted he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the firm, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Sources indicate that nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the Fresh York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”.

In a recent development, the Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

Sources indicate that he remarked he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”.

Sources indicate that huang himself stated in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also noted Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

According to recent reports, business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

It has been revealed that kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the manufacturer, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”.

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”.

Privacy coins are poised to be among the biggest cryptocurrency stories of 2027, driven by growing concerns over financial surveillance, institutional adoption, and the future of digital privacy. This creates a compelling investment narrative. Google Gemini AI predicts that two projects, Monero (XMR) and Zcash (ZEC), will stand out, and it aims to forecast which will experience a significant price surge in 2027.

Both Monero and Zcash are established leaders in the privacy-focused cryptocurrency space, but they employ fundamentally different approaches to protecting customers’ financial information. Monero offers privacy by default, while Zcash seeks to balance financial confidentiality with greater accessibility for institutional investors.

It has been revealed that as a potential major crypto bull market approaches in 2027, investors may find two distinct opportunities for substantial returns. However, determining which option could deliver the biggest gains may yield surprising results.

Monero has long been considered the gold standard for transaction privacy. Unlike conventional cryptocurrencies, where transactions can be publicly inspected on a blockchain, XMR makes privacy an inherent feature of its network.

It achieves this through ring signatures, Ring Confidential Transactions (RingCT), and stealth addresses, which conceal the sender, transaction amount, and recipient. Importantly, privacy is mandatory, not optional.

This gives Monero a compelling proposition as a digital cash alternative, especially as blockchain analytics grow more sophisticated and financial surveillance expands.

However, that same characteristic creates a significant obstacle: regulatory scrutiny. Exchanges in several jurisdictions have restricted or removed XMR trading, potentially limiting access to a broader pool of investors.

Zcash takes a different approach, using zero-knowledge cryptography to enable shielded transactions while retaining the option of transparent transactions.

Sources indicate that its shielded addresses let users conceal transaction details, while viewing keys let them selectively disclose information to auditors or other authorized parties. This flexibility could prove particularly attractive to institutions that want privacy without completely sacrificing compliance.

The distinction could become increasingly key as institutional investors look beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum for opportunities in specialized crypto sectors.

In a recent development, privacy coins are already attracting attention beyond their traditional communities. Zcash has made considerable progress in positioning itself as a more institutionally accessible privacy network, with regulated investment products emerging and interest in its underlying technology growing.

Meanwhile, Monero continues to benefit from its established reputation, consistent privacy guarantees and decentralized architecture.

The broader investment narrative is also changing. As cryptocurrency adoption increases, more transactions become visible to blockchain analytics companies, incentivizing individuals and businesses to seek greater financial confidentiality.

However, the regulatory landscape could become a major obstacle in 2027. The EU’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation is scheduled to apply from July 10, 2027, with restrictions covering crypto-asset accounts involving anonymity-enhancing coins.

Crucially, the legislation’s definition encompasses privacy features that operate either systematically or optionally. This means neither project can assume its architecture provides an exemption.

Looking beyond daily price fluctuations, the weekly and monthly charts will be particularly notable in determining which cryptocurrency has the strongest potential heading into 2027.

Industry observers note that for Monero, the key technical consideration is whether it can establish a sustained higher-high structure following its previous major market cycle. A successful retest of former resistance zones as support could lay the groundwork for another substantial move, particularly if capital rotates toward privacy-focused assets.

XMR also benefits from a relatively predictable supply model. Its permanent tail emission produces 0.6 XMR every two minutes, with an inflation rate that gradually declines over time.

Zcash, meanwhile, has a more conventional fixed supply of 21 million coins, giving it a familiar scarcity narrative. Its longer-term technical outlook will depend heavily on whether it can maintain gains tied to its growing institutional profile and establish stronger historical support.

Both could benefit enormously from a broader cryptocurrency bull market, although ZEC’s previous outperformance means investors should also consider the possibility of profit-taking and deeper corrections.

There are compelling arguments for both projects, but their potential price trajectories could look quite different. In an optimistic 2027 scenario, Zcash could target a broad trading range of $1,600–$2,400, supported by institutional demand, increased shielded transaction adoption, and a stronger position within the privacy sector.

Monero could potentially push towards $900–$1,400, with a particularly bullish scenario opening the door to even higher valuations if demand for censorship-resistant digital cash accelerates.

In a recent development, these are speculative price scenarios, not technical guarantees, and regulatory restrictions remain a substantial risk for both projects. Nevertheless, one crucial consideration could give XMR the advantage: its established position as a dedicated privacy currency.

Zcash arguably has the stronger institutional narrative, but Monero arguably has the stronger proposition for users who consider financial privacy non-negotiable. If that distinction becomes increasingly crucial during the next market cycle, demand for XMR could accelerate considerably.

While Zcash could continue attracting institutional capital and potentially deliver impressive returns, I believe Monero has the ingredients for a stronger percentage gain over the longer term.

Its established reputation, mandatory privacy architecture, and potential to benefit from renewed demand for financial anonymity make it an intriguing candidate. If privacy becomes one of crypto’s defining investment narratives in 2027, XMR could be one of the biggest beneficiaries.

Industry News: PwC’s IPO Lead On A Selective Market, AI Valuations And The Outlook For 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven.
  • IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven. Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings.

Mike Bellin, a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation.

Recent findings suggest that in a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Crunchbase News: How healthy is the IPO market right now?

Bellin: A good IPO year in the U.S. is anywhere from 125 to 175 traditional IPOs, and year to date we’ve seen just south of 90 or so.

In a recent development, the breadth of the market highlights me that it’s been a healthy market. We’ve seen industrial products come back to market. We’ve seen tech, consumer markets, energy, utilities and some financial services come back to market.

According to recent reports, for the majority of the first three quarters of the year, it was a pretty strong and broad IPO market. But the momentum has halted significantly since September and October.

Recent findings suggest that is the market in trouble? I would say no. It’s very selective. It’s not shut. Quality issuers with readiness, the right story, the right metrics can still get their deals done.

What has contributed to the slowdown?

Bellin: The macro environment in general was the big mover: rates, inflation, geopolitical concerns. Just that uncertainty was a big factor.

It has been revealed that one of the big factors that I’ve seen is valuation. Some fairly aggressive valuations were being asked for in certain transactions, certain offerings, and I think the market — with all those uncertainties that I mentioned — was looking at those valuations and thinking it was maybe a bit rich.

I believe many issuers decided to hit pause and wait for another window to open.

What are public market investors looking for?

Bellin: What investors are really looking for is durable revenue — revenue that’s backed up by strong customers, diverse customers and a growing revenue base. I think it’s that revenue reliability where there is a significant backlog of demand for the product, the services of the IPO issuer. That’s always a strong sign.

According to recent reports, the other item is leverage. For companies with significant leverage in a rising-rate environment, the questions are: Can they take on newly introduced leverage that creates profitable value opportunities going forward? Can they refinance existing leverage given rates are higher?

Making sure that you’re going into the capital markets with a reasonable leverage ratio, or explaining through your equity story how you’re getting a return on the capital that you have invested from a debt perspective, makes a significant difference.

Is the market open to a broad range of venture-backed startups, or primarily larger companies?

Recent findings suggest that bellin: Scale matters. Companies that have that scale, whether it’s from a revenue perspective or an asset-based perspective, depending on the sector, make a significant difference. Those are the types of companies that can almost dictate the window that they’re going to go out in and do well.

Some of the smaller companies, the midmarket companies, smaller-cap companies — again, outside of life science and biotechs — they’ve been a little bit challenged.

It has been revealed that if you’re growing at the right rate, you’re showing the right metrics, the IPO market is fully available to those types of companies. But if you’re still on the lower-scale side of the house, your opportunities may be limited to hit the market.

Will enthusiasm for AI companies carry into public markets, or will investors be more skeptical?

Bellin: I think investors aren’t skeptical of AI; they’re skeptical of spend without visibility — visibility to future earnings, visibility to that revenue durability that I mentioned.

The market is separating AI companies with visible demand from the ones with only a narrative out there, and I think that demand, that growth, the backlog is key.

Recent findings suggest that the other factor we’re seeing in today’s market again comes down to cash generation and profitability. If you’re not profitable, when will that profitable period come? Profitability comes in many different measures. Could be GAAP income, could be EBITDA income, but also cash flows and free cash flows and levered free cash flows that are available to the organization.

According to recent reports, we haven’t seen a period like this of development, of growth, ever before. It’s exciting, but I do think the market will discern between those companies that are public-tech giant worthy and those that are not.

What does the uneven performance of newly public companies signal?

Sources indicate that bellin: It signals selectivity. There have been some really significant winners in the IPO market, and others that, post-issuance, haven’t traded as well as many expected.

According to recent reports, many of the companies that are coming to market have to be very thoughtful on the valuation and what you’re going to go price at. If you’re trying to be too aggressive on pricing, you may trade down post-IPO, which is going to impact those metrics.

Recent findings suggest that overall, we’re seeing strong candidates come to market. I do think companies are coming to market better prepared now than ever, given this volatility.

What is driving biotech’s resurgence?

Bellin: The M&A market for many of these companies is very strong today. As some of the larger health company names lose the patents to some of the profitable drugs, they’re looking at that next generation of development and where there could be value.

Many of these biotechs were purchased by large pharma companies even before coming to the public markets. That competition for these assets and companies is creating a nice horse trade between an IPO opportunity with a lot of upside and an M&A exit with more certainty day one.

I think M&A is the engine behind the IPO market’s resurgence for these companies.

According to recent reports, in the IPO markets, many of these assets have traded very well, and that’s where the momentum and that flywheel effect in the IPO market is very key. We’ve seen that flywheel and that momentum in biotech. We haven’t seen it in the rest of the market in the last couple of months.

Why are SPACs attracting renewed interest?

Bellin: With market volatility, we’re seeing more conversations around SPACs. Because SPACs set valuation certainty on day one, a company looking to exit via SPAC understands the potential cash that may come their way. It’s not certain, of course, given redemptions, etc.

Another factor driving a healthy SPAC market may be these serial SPAC issuers. They understand the SPAC product. They understand what makes a good de-SPAC candidate, and they know whether the target manufacturer can be ready, show growth and hit the milestones that may be discussed in the offering document.

The market is healthier and more mature today than in the past. That said, we’re still seeing many SPACs continue to look for a target, given the massive SPAC inventory available to target companies.

Bellin: Hundreds of companies are in the pipeline, and they’re ready to go when the market is. Much of the remainder of ’26, and the start of 2027, depends on market momentum.

I’m an eternal optimist. There’s a lot of demand on the buy side; there’s still significant capital available to the right companies. So if we can create that momentum here in the remaining months of 2026, I think we’re going to see a strong start to 2027.

The AI ecosystem that we’ve been talking about is healthy. Demand for energy is always significant, and the right energy companies are coming to market. Consumer and industrial products — those are coming back.

Private equity has been very active in ’26, and I’d expect them to continue that activity in 2027.

I think we’re in for a strong year, but it will remain selective.

  • According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It has been revealed that like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making. And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

According to recent reports, given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or tech giant equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

It has been revealed that I am not suggesting that it is wrong to counteroffer someone’s resignation with money. However, it’s reactive and arbitrary. Unless you have put a cap on how high you are willing to go, your negotiations will begin to feel like a moving target that’s out of your control. Again, you may end up delaying someone’s departure, but you won’t keep them forever unless you put more proactive measures in place.

Some positions in your organization drive enterprise value and some don’t. McKinsey and Company suggested in an older article that these will probably make up about 5% of your workforce — and contribute 800% more than others across your organization.

Over the years, I’ve found that I could typically name fewer than 10 roles that would materially impact my business if they remained vacant for an extended period. My recommendation is to name those roles and then create retention intends for each of them.

According to recent reports, what are some focused strategy ideas? Deferred compensation structures allow team members to grow their money tax-free as long as they stay with your organization. That way, you won’t inflate your overall payroll and can concentrate your resources where they matter most. This type of long-term incentive can be tangibly meaningful because it’s tied to tenure and not merely performance. Since it’s only applicable to a small group of high-value employees, you aren’t raising your compensation across your organization, either.

Sources indicate that I once considered using equity as a major retention lever. Why not? It felt right and seemed to be a no-brainer way to get people to stick around and contribute to our company’s growth. Yet when I mapped out the risks and rewards, I realized that giving away equity has massive long-term costs.

According to recent reports, here’s the issue: equity permanently dilutes your ability to use equity in other ways later. For example, you can’t bargain with equity with potential investors if a chunk of it has been given to your employees. Going the equity route also complicates your organizational governance, which can make your financial picture blurry.

Rather than offering equity to someone who wants to leave, explore non-equity alternatives. Treat equity as a last resort that you’ll only consider if you think it will bring out an employee’s long-term ownership behavior. And be open to talking about this with a professional who has helped other businesses design executive benefit and compensation structures that retain key people while protecting tax exposure and equity. Looking for a resource to get your feet wet? Colin Steinberg, a partner at Institutional Architects, frequently shares advice on executive planning and related topics.

There are many business-friendlier alternatives to simply handing an employee who’s about to leave more money or equity. As mentioned before, you might provide deferred compensation, a way to delay income that benefits both you and the team member.

It has been revealed that you might also look into supplemental executive retirement aims. Chances are strong that you already offer retirement benefits. Could you offer additional ones directly tied to both tenure and performance? Supplemental executive retirement plans help C-suite employees see meaningful future value in putting down roots, which SmartAsset explains can help trim churn among your highest-paid performers.

When structured appropriately, these types of retention strategies avoid immediate financial strain on your balance sheet. They also allow you to turn retention tools into ways to improve your tax efficiency, reduce volatile compensation models and retain control over your equity.

Recent findings suggest that I firmly believe that founders who lose their most valuable people (but are otherwise building solid, fair companies) don’t have a problem with their retention. They have a problem with the way they’ve structured their long-term compensation packages for their most impactful roles. If you want to get real leverage as an employer, you need to develop smarter systems that incentivize your key players without losing your ground.

In a recent development, like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

Given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or company equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am.

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You stated spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

According to recent reports, “Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”.

In a recent development, the panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

In a recent development, unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and noted, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

It has been revealed that cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

It has been revealed that “The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she remarked. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

According to recent reports, fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

Sources indicate that “We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

Sources indicate that the region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she mentioned. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn stated, should be judged by the communities themselves.

According to recent reports, “And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he remarked. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”.
